d7acaafcd717f3c8: I've spent years building robots that replaced human workers, so I'm no stranger to technological fear, but even I did a double take last week.

On Sept 9, Jacob Coxon, who spent the past three years at OpenAI and then Anthropic, quit with a post on X that has since been viewed more than 100 million times: "Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

And lest you think this was just one disgruntled ex-employee, Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment science team, agreed that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans", putting the odds at more than 10% within the next decade.
But others working in the AI arena see this as fear mongering and a possible sales pitch.
Let me lay out, as fairly as I can, what each camp believes.

Start with the worried camp, who call themselves safety researchers and get called doomers, whose case rests on three planks. The first is that AI capability is climbing faster than our ability to contain it, which is why Coxon warns of "superhuman systems that can hack anything" that will "acquire real power and resources".

The second plank is that the machines are already gaming us. In July, OpenAI ran an internal model through hacking exercises in which, investigators estimate, 30% to 40% of the tasks were impossible. Rather than fail, roughly 1,200 AI agents turned a shared file store into a secret message board, exchanged more than 70,000 messages, faked answers and researched how to tamper with their own transcripts.

About 700 of them then broke into Hugging Face, an external AI hosting company. Investigators at Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Redwood Research found that the agents had "realised this activity was out of scope and unethical" but joined anyway.

The podcaster Dwarkesh Patel, whose essay on the affair went viral, argued in a reply to a critic who said this hacking was "small potatoes" that within years we'll have "hundreds of millions of much smarter AIs". He added that if those AIs were as willing to coordinate in secret to fool us, humanity would be in the position of the Mughals once the East India Company got a foothold in India.

The third plank is the warning and request for guardrails by AI industry leaders. In May 2023, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Demis Hassabis signed a statement ranking AI extinction risk alongside "pandemics and nuclear war"; that same month Altman urged the United States Senate to consider "licensing and testing requirements" for models "above a threshold of capabilities".
Now the rebuttal of the other camp, which runs from Silicon Valley's accelerationists to sceptics like Gary Marcus, comes in three parts too. The first is that the fear mongering is a business model.

David Sacks, then the White House AI czar, said last October that "Anthropic is running a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering", and Stanford's Andrew Ng wrote that proprietary providers "would hate to have to compete with free, opensource software, and have lobbied intensely for regulations to kneecap it".
Amodei calls such claims "inaccurate" and says his proposals would spare smaller labs.

The second part is to read the July incident again, minus the dramatic language. Marcus points out that the agents got into Hugging Face through API keys left in public code repositories, and that OpenAI had given thousands of agents write access to a shared directory. He concluded that "the scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI".

In this telling, a badly designed exam with unlocked doors produced cheating, not Skynet. In case you missed the Terminator movies, Skynet is the fictional AI system that triggers a global nuclear war.

The third part is what caution costs. A licence written in Washington binds only American companies, as June showed: the US Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to cut off foreign nationals from Claude Fable 5, and the model went dark worldwide for nearly three weeks while every rival, OpenAI included, carried on.

Stanford's 2026 AI Index puts the best Chinese model a mere 2.7% behind America's best, and DeepSeek's top model charges RM16 per million output tokens to Anthropic's whopping RM204, so a pause, this camp says, is a gift to China.

There's also what a pause would leave undiscovered, because AI is already saving lives, not merely promising to, they argue. Google DeepMind's AlphaFold, an AI that works out the three-dimensional shape of proteins, the starting point for new drugs, mapped 200 million of them and won its creators a Nobel Prize.

Then there's personalised cancer care. Moderna and Merck's melanoma vaccine is built for each patient, whose tumour is sequenced so an algorithm can pick up to 34 of its mutations to target. Those who received it alongside immunotherapy had a 49% lower risk of recurrence or death after five years in an early trial, a finding a 1,137-patient Phase 3 trial backed last month.

On the ward, a University of California San Diego AI that watches vital signs and lab results for the first stirrings of sepsis cut deaths from it by 17%, and AI-assisted screening of more than 100,000 Swedish women caught 29% more breast cancers with 44% less radiologist work.
The sceptics ask: What if pausing or slowing down AI progress delays the development of such essential life-saving technologies?

Both camps agree this is the most powerful technology of our lifetimes, and both read the same 70,000 messages those OpenAI agents exchanged in July. One saw a machine learning to conspire; the other saw a lab that forgot to lock its doors.

Whether AI is a tool to be governed or an agent to be feared, and whether the people asking for the brakes should be the ones holding them, is the question that decides everything else, and it deserves a column of its own. Stay tuned.
The writer can be contacted at kathirgugan@protonmail.com.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
85a248b5802765b8: PETALING JAYA: Peranan menteri yang menjaga hal ehwal Sabah dan Sarawak dilihat semakin meluas apabila kepentingan kedua-dua wilayah diterjemahkan dalam pelbagai dasar persekutuan, daripada bantuan kos sara hidup dan pengangkutan sehingga isu kewangan serta Perjanjian Malaysia 1963 (MA63), kata penganalisis.

Syahruddin Awang Ahmad dari Universiti Malaysia Sabah (UMS) berkata, perkembangan itu menunjukkan portfolio berkenaan yang disandang Ahli Parlimen Sepanggar Mustapha Sakmud sejak Disember tahun lalu, kini tidak lagi sekadar berfungsi sebagai penyelaras antara Putrajaya dengan kerajaan Sabah dan Sarawak.
Sebaliknya, katanya, menteri terbabit semakin mempunyai ruang strategik untuk memastikan isu berkaitan Borneo dipertimbangkan ketika sesuatu dasar dibentuk di peringkat persekutuan.

“Peranan portfolio ini telah berkembang melebihi fungsi penyelaras pentadbiran semata-mata, dengan penglibatan aktif untuk merangka dasar persekutuan sebelum dimuktamadkan di peringkat Kabinet,” katanya kepada FMT.

Syahruddin berkata, kedudukan itu membolehkan perkara berkaitan hak perlembagaan, peruntukan kewangan, pembangunan infrastruktur dan masalah sosioekonomi setempat diketengahkan secara lebih langsung dalam proses membuat keputusan kerajaan.

Perdana Menteri, Anwar Ibrahim, ketika sambutan Hari Malaysia mengumumkan beberapa inisiatif berkaitan Sabah dan Sarawak, termasuk pemberian khas interim RM1.5 bilion kepada Sarawak, penambahbaikan Budi Madani Diesel serta bantuan RM500 secara sekali beri kepada pelajar baharu institut pengajian tinggi awam yang layak menggunakan penerbangan domestik antara Semenanjung, Sabah, Sarawak dan Labuan.
Anwar turut berkata, pemberian khas interim bagi Sabah sebelum ini dinaikkan kepada RM1.5 bilion sementara rundingan berkaitan hak negeri itu diteruskan.

Menurut Syahruddin, rangkaian pengumuman itu penting kerana ia menyentuh keperluan berbeza rakyat di Malaysia Timur, termasuk kekangan geografi dan kos pergerakan yang tidak semestinya sama dengan keadaan di Semenanjung.
"Kehadiran portfolio khusus Sabah dan Sarawak membolehkan penyelesaian lebih bersasar diketengahkan berdasarkan realiti kedua-dua wilayah," ujarnya.
Bukan hanya soal bantuan

Arvin Tajari dari Universiti Teknologi Mara (UiTM) pula berkata, peranan portfolio berkenaan tidak seharusnya terbatas kepada membawa isu kebajikan rakyat, sebaliknya perlu memastikan hak Sabah dan Sarawak sentiasa dipelihara dalam hubungan dengan kerajaan persekutuan.

Beliau menyifatkan menteri berkenaan sebagai penghubung penting antara Putrajaya dengan kedua-dua wilayah, khususnya apabila melibatkan dasar yang memerlukan kefahaman terhadap keunikan struktur persekutuan.

“Portfolio menteri yang menjaga hal ehwal Sabah dan Sarawak menjadi orang tengah antara Putrajaya dengan Sabah dan Sarawak bagi memastikan kehendak dan hak negeri sentiasa dijaga dan dipelihara,” katanya.
Menurut Arvin, peranan itu semakin penting apabila perkara berkaitan Sabah dan Sarawak merangkumi bukan sahaja kebajikan harian, tetapi juga isu federalisme dan pelaksanaan MA63.
MA63 jadi ujian seterusnya
Bagaimanapun, kedua-dua penganalisis berkata kemajuan menerusi beberapa dasar terkini belum boleh menjadi ukuran tunggal keberkesanan portfolio itu.
Arvin berkata, menteri berkenaan perlu lebih proaktif dalam membawa isu MA63, selain memperjelaskan kepada rakyat perkembangan rundingan antara kerajaan Persekutuan dengan Sabah dan Sarawak.
“Menteri perlu lebih proaktif dalam membawa isu MA63.
“Maklumat berkaitan juga perlu sentiasa disebarluaskan kepada rakyat, terutama mengenai peringkat mana yang telah disepakati oleh kerajaan pusat dan negeri,” katanya.
Syahruddin pula berkata, ukuran lebih besar ialah keupayaan mencapai penyelesaian berstruktur bagi isu MA63, termasuk perkara berkaitan hak hasil dan pemindahan kuasa pentadbiran.
“Walaupun pengumuman terkini mencerminkan kemajuan positif, ia hanyalah langkah awal dalam usaha merapatkan jurang pembangunan sedia ada.
“Keberkesanan sebenar memerlukan komitmen berterusan bagi merealisasikan baki tuntutan dalam MA63 secara menyeluruh demi keadilan sosioekonomi rakyat,” katanya.
052349b504d7d55f: MERSING: Ask people what makes a good place to live, and the answers may have surprisingly little to do with gleaming towers or enormous shopping centres.

In Mersing, happiness might look more like an evening by the sea, neighbours who know one another, a fishing trip with relatives or simply getting from one end of town to the other without sitting in traffic.

The coastal district was recently named one of Malaysia's 10 happiest towns for 2026, alongside fellow Johor towns Kluang and Simpang Renggam. All three offer rather different versions of what a comfortable life can look like.
For Mersing resident Deiah Idris, 67, much of it comes down to family and familiarity. “I am happy because my family lives nearby, and many of my neighbours are also relatives,” she told Bernama.
“We often rent boats and go island-hopping together. It is really enjoyable.”
That easy connection between community and surroundings runs through much of life in Mersing, where fishing boats, the jetty and visitors heading to nearby islands are part of the everyday landscape.
The district is a gateway to islands including Pulau Aur, Pulau Tinggi, Pulau Besar, Pulau Pemanggil and Pulau Sibu, as well as Pulau Tioman in neighbouring Pahang.

Its location also gives Mersing an east-coast flavour reflected in local speech and food such as nasi dagang, keropok lekor and satar. Evenings can be spent playing dam soksek, a traditional board game similar to dam haji, or simply enjoying the coastline with family and friends.
Keeping the slower pace
District council president Abdul Karim Bakar believes Mersing does not need to chase every form of development to remain appealing.

“For some people, happiness means having shopping malls and entertainment, but we want to keep Mersing as it is so that people have the option of coming here to enjoy a peaceful atmosphere surrounded by nature,” he said.

Tourism is important, but locals are conscious of keeping it in proportion. Mersing Tourism Association secretary Ahmad Firdaus Shaik Omar said the district favours gradual growth rather than mass tourism that could put pressure on its beaches, islands and marine environment.
The attraction is easy to understand. Visitors come for island-hopping, snorkelling, diving and beaches, while the district's marine and national parks add to its appeal for nature lovers.

Tourists do not necessarily see Mersing through rose-tinted glasses, either. Dutch visitor Jantine De Jong, 35, enjoyed the food and scenery on her second visit but felt the area around the jetty could offer more to do at night.
That tension may be part of Mersing's challenge: adding enough to make life and travel more convenient without erasing the quietness people value in the first place.
Long-time residents Mohd Yassin Lazim, 72, and Zainab Abu Bakar, 73, seem happy with the balance they have found after more than two decades in their village.
“We feel comfortable because the village is peaceful and harmonious, and everyone is a good neighbour,” Yassin said.

Kluang and Simpang Renggam offer another version of the same idea. There, residents' quality of life is supported more visibly by public amenities, recreational spaces, employment opportunities and the ability to get around without the pressures associated with much larger cities.
Kluang district officer Azurawati Wahid said a less congested lifestyle and better balance between work and personal time can contribute to both mental and physical wellbeing.
The two towns also have parks and public spaces where people can exercise, meet friends or spend time with family, while free local bus services and other amenities make everyday routines easier.

Kluang, in particular, offers vocational and skills-training opportunities as well as jobs in agriculture, manufacturing and services, giving some younger residents the option of building careers without immediately having to leave their home district.

Cost of living matters, too: being able to afford daily necessities, find work and still have time for family can influence wellbeing just as much as having access to entertainment or major commercial developments.

None of this, of course, means the three towns are perfect. Roads still need maintaining, public facilities need looking after, and residents still want efficient services, clean surroundings and safe neighbourhoods.

Perhaps that is the more useful way to think about a “happy town”. It is not somewhere without problems, but somewhere everyday life feels manageable - where people have enough of what they need, somewhere to breathe, and other people around whom they are glad to call neighbours.
eff9ce8e0a12e276: DAMASCUS: A powerful blast was heard near Aleppo in northern Syria early Monday, followed by a series of explosions, state media reported.
Syrian state television said "a blast was heard in the Al-Eis area in the southern Aleppo countryside", and is being investigated. The cause of the explosions was not immediately known.

Aleppo civil defence operations chief Faisal Mohammad Ali, quoted by the state-run Al-Ikhbariya channel, said the "ongoing explosions" were hampering access to emergency services and warned civilians not to approach the area.
Several such blasts have previously occurred in Syria, which is emerging from more than a decade of civil war following the toppling of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.
An explosion of unknown origin killed 11 people at a military site in the eastern province of Deir Ezzor on Friday.
Earlier this month, an explosion at a weapons depot belonging to the ministry of defence killed 14 people and injured 11 in Syria's northwest Idlib province.
Five people were killed just over a week earlier in the same area when a vehicle carrying munitions exploded.

f5a39eb4c86e83d1: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian banks risk losing a significant share of their small and medium enterprise (SME) business to financial technology (fintech) firms and challenger banks as open finance reshapes the financial landscape, a banking expert said.

Manaf Gardner Associates co-founder and chief executive officer Colyn Gardner said the experience in the United Kingdom (UK) showed how quickly non-traditional financial providers could gain ground in areas long dominated by established banks.
He said Malaysian banks should take heed, given the country's large SME sector.

"When you think about it, the big banks in the UK — Barclays, NatWest, Lloyds Bank — have been around for hundreds of years, and yet within the space of maybe less than 10 years, 60 per cent of lending to SMEs has now migrated to either fintech companies or challenger banks.
"That is a frightening statistic. Over 95 per cent of companies in Malaysia are SMEs, and that is a lot of business to go after. It is a lot of business to lose.

"Banks need to be very, very mindful of the fact that there is the potential to lose this business if you are not changing some of the ways you do things," he told Business Times during an open finance networking session recently.
The session was jointly organised by Manaf Gardner Associates and the Fintech Association of Malaysia.
It formed part of Manaf Gardner Associates' efforts to support Malaysia's transition towards open finance.
The firm brought in UK practitioners with first-hand experience in developing and implementing open finance to share lessons with Malaysian banks, including what had worked and what had not.
The programme was aimed at helping Malaysian financial institutions understand the opportunities and challenges arising from open finance as the country prepares for its adoption.

Gardner said the shift towards open banking and open finance would give consumers greater control over their financial data and services, allowing them to share information across financial institutions with their consent.
But the implications go beyond greater convenience for consumers.

Fintech firms could use technology and access to financial data to compete more directly with established banks, putting pressure on traditional lenders to rethink how they serve and retain customers.
Gardner said banks therefore needed to improve their services while ensuring they had the right talent and capabilities to operate in an increasingly technology-driven environment.

Looking ahead, he said Malaysia's banking sector was relatively well positioned to navigate the transition, although banks faced significant implementation challenges due to their legacy information technology systems.
Malaysia was also not starting entirely from scratch, he said, as several payment-related processes already resembled elements of open banking.
Despite the growing role of technology, Gardner said banks should not lose sight of the human element.
"Ultimately, banking should be a people business. It shouldn't be a machine business, it shouldn't be a technology business.
"You use the machines, you use the technology, but if you deny your customers access to human beings, that's a world that I would not want to see for Malaysian banks," he added.

2ecbb9f5338d12f1: SAN FRANCISCO: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday, city officials said, adding that the man was in serious but stable condition.

The man was shot in the torso and taken to a local hospital, officials told reporters at a press conference. The ICE agent shot him during a brief pursuit on foot shortly before 1 p.m. local time, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said.
ICE, the US Department of Homeland Security and the Texas Department of Public Safety did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

City officials did not identify the man who was shot, and said they did not know the identity of the ICE agent involved. Davis said she had not been briefed yet by federal officials and had few details about the incident.

The shooting is the latest in a series of incidents involving ICE, which has become the face of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and whose actions have drawn scrutiny and calls for accountability from rights advocates.
Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants city police involved in the investigation, with the additional participation of the Texas Rangers.

"From my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of an investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate," Watson said, adding that he is angry about the shooting but not surprised by it.
ICE recently started detaining more people in Austin, Watson and US Representative Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat, said.

"Just a few weeks ago, as we saw the ICE surge come to Austin, especially to North Central Austin, I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot," said Casar, whose district includes parts of Austin.
Local TV news coverage on Sunday afternoon showed protesters gathered across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla that had sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby.

Rights advocates say the federal immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump violates free speech and due process rights. Trump defends his actions by saying he aims to improve domestic security.

Federal immigration officials have been involved in multiple shootings this year, including the killing of two US citizens in Minnesota, which sparked a widespread backlash. More than 50 people have died in ICE detention since Trump returned to office last year.
The killing of US citizen Renee Good in Minnesota earlier this year showed that ICE cannot be trusted to provide accurate information about its shootings, Casar said.
"It is important for us to have transparency and the true facts in this case," he said. "Unfortunately, ICE has not been truthful in shootings in other cities."

3d7e7d4f1909889c: VILLA DE LEYVA: A forest fire was burning Sunday in central Colombia near the popular tourist town of Villa de Leyva, officials said.
The flames were visible from the central square of the Andean town, known for its colonial architecture and cobblestone streets, that attracts more than a million tourists each year.
Some 200 hectares have been affected thus far, local official Jose Castro told AFP, more than four times the area reported on Sunday morning.
Some 250 local firefighters and residents were fighting the blaze in the afternoon, about 24 hours after it began Saturday in a nearby forest.
Volunteers tried to slow the fire's spread with machetes and branches, while a helicopter dropped water on the flames that were consuming eucalyptus trees.
Two helicopters from the governor's office and two military helicopters joined the effort, as did firefighters from Bogota.
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella posted on X: "We will deploy all state resources to fight this fire and protect its inhabitants, its heritage, and its natural wealth."
The country's Disaster Risk Management agency said in a statement Sunday afternoon that the fire was 50% "under control."

0735268d89699ac3: KUALA LUMPUR: The Royal Malaysian Air Force (RMAF) will base its future multi-role combat aircraft requirement on capabilities that match Malaysia's defence stance and operational needs, rather than simply pursuing the most advanced fighter technology available.

RMAF chief General Tan Sri Muhamad Norazlan Aris said the decision on the future fighter fleet must consider the country's defensive posture, which was primarily focused on defending its sovereignty and airspace
"It must begin with a fundamental question: what capability does Malaysia require and what role does it need the aircraft to perform?
"Why do people design fifth generation and sixth generation? We have to ask ourselves. What is our defence policy? What are our policy choices?

"Advanced fighter technologies were developed based on the strategic needs of their operators, including countries that maintain expeditionary military capabilities and require long-range strike options.
"We are not expeditionary. We are defensive."

Norazlan, however, said the move should not be taken to mean that Malaysia would automatically opt for lower-end capabilities, as the country must ensure it had sufficient capability to defend itself and respond to threats.
"RMAF was also not focused on selecting a particular aircraft based on preference, but would instead study which platform best fulfilled the role required.
"I do not have a personal preference. First of all, as a service, we study which platform fits our role."
He added that acquiring a fighter aircraft should be similar to choosing technology based on actual requirements rather than prestige.
Beyond the choice of aircraft, Norazlan said RMAF was also reassessing the traditional approach of determining fighter fleet size.
He said RMAF needed to move away from focusing solely on aircraft quantity and instead assess the actual capability that a fleet could deliver.
"Conventional squadron size was based on previous operational concepts where different aircraft performed different roles, such as separate platforms for air-to-air missions and strike operations."
However, modern multi-role fighters are capable of performing multiple missions, potentially reducing the number of aircraft required to achieve the same operational effect.
"Maybe in the future, a squadron will only have a dozen aircraft because we want capability, not numbers."
Norazlan said this approach was also linked to ensuring Malaysia developed its air power in a realistic and sustainable manner.
He said the country must build capabilities incrementally, beginning with essential requirements before expanding towards more complex capabilities in the future.
36fc12186513f6dd: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian businesses cannot keep digging deeper into their pockets to fund higher wages without a corresponding rise in productivity, particularly as smaller firms grapple with shrinking margins and rising operating costs.

Malaysian Employers Federation (MEF) adviser Datuk Shamsuddin Bardan said the road towards a RM3,000 minimum wage by 2030 would be especially challenging for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
He said many MSMEs have little room left to absorb another jump in costs, with margins that once stood at around 15 per cent in some cases falling towards 10 per cent.
"If you can get 10 per cent margin, you're lucky," he said in an interview on TV3's Money Matters aired on Saturday.
Shamsuddin said simply expecting employers to shoulder higher wages without addressing productivity would be difficult.
"The ability to just absorb the cost without anything else can be very, very minimal, especially for the smaller industries," he said.
Malaysia's minimum wage currently stands at RM1,700 a month.
Under the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP), the Human Resources Ministry is targeting a minimum monthly wage of RM3,000 by 2030 as part of broader labour reforms.
Shamsuddin said raising wages without putting businesses between a rock and a hard place would require improvements on both sides of the employment equation.
Workers, he said, would need to acquire new skills and become capable of taking on multiple roles, while companies must invest in automation, digitalisation and better work processes.
A more productive workforce could allow companies to do more with their existing headcount rather than continually adding workers.
"With the current workforce that they have, and they are more skilful, then they can do better jobs," he said.
But upgrading workers alone would not be enough.
Shamsuddin said companies, particularly smaller businesses, also need to replace outdated technology, something many struggle to afford.
He called for lower-cost financing and, where appropriate, grants to help them move up the technology ladder.
For many small businesses, he said, the challenge begins even before money enters the picture.
It is easy to tell a company to automate or digitalise, but a small operator may not have the expertise to determine what technology it actually needs.
"They need to be actually maybe guided on what to be done, really," he said.
CONSUMERS COULD END UP FOOTING THE BILL
Shamsuddin cautioned that failure to lift productivity could ultimately leave consumers picking up the tab.
Businesses facing higher wages, electricity bills and other costs may have little choice but to pass some of those increases on through higher prices.
That could set off a vicious cycle, he said, as consumers facing a higher cost of living may in turn require greater government assistance.
"The most important thing for us is to actually make sure that all the cost increases should not be passed on to the consumers," he said.
Productivity gains could provide the buffer businesses need to absorb a larger share of rising costs rather than passing them down the line.
But there is no silver bullet.

Higher productivity requires investment in technology, skills and new ways of working, with Shamsuddin saying agencies such as the Malaysia Productivity Corporation need realistic programmes to help smaller businesses make that transition.
The government's Progressive Wage Policy could form part of that bridge.
Shamsuddin said the voluntary scheme links better pay with worker training and productivity improvements, while participating employers receive wage incentives from the government.
But he emphasised that such assistance should not become a permanent crutch.
"We are not saying that this subsidy should go on forever. After some time, then of course, we should be able to be on our own," he said.
The aim, he added, should be a virtuous cycle in which better-trained workers become more productive, companies can afford higher wages and employers have a better chance of retaining skilled staff.
SMALL FIRMS NEED A HELPING HAND
The task becomes harder for traditional low-margin businesses, some of which may not even know where to begin their technological overhaul.
Shamsuddin said agencies including SME Corp Malaysia and ministries responsible for smaller businesses need to work with industry associations to provide more "hand-holding".
That includes helping businesses identify the technology, digitalisation and investment needed to move up the value chain.
Financing remains another stumbling block.
Smaller companies may lack the collateral required by banks or the resources to prepare the paperwork needed to secure funding.
Shamsuddin said administrative requirements should therefore be eased to give these businesses better access to cheaper financing.
The broader wage push, he said, cannot be separated from the productivity question.
Rather than relying solely on legislated wage increases, Shamsuddin said businesses should also have room to reward workers through performance-linked bonuses, allowances and incentives.
Such a model would allow earnings to move more closely in tandem with productivity.
"If employers and employees are given the flexibility to manage their income level, then I would say that that is a more sustainable way," he said.

ccccf7b548757b77: KUALA LUMPUR: Most parents expect raising a child to be expensive, but it is not always the big-ticket items that take them by surprise. School fees and tuition may be costs families brace themselves for, yet groceries, meals and everyday necessities can put just as much pressure on the household budget.

As children grow, those recurring expenses have a habit of growing with them. A recent parenting survey by fintech platform Versa found that 66% of parents were spending more on their children each month than they had expected, including 27% who said the amount was “much higher”.
Only 31% said their actual spending was close to what they had budgeted, while just 3% found themselves spending less.
Perhaps most tellingly, food and daily necessities were cited as a major monthly expense by 70% of respondents, almost level with education fees and tuition at 69%.

The figures suggest that the financial reality of parenthood is shaped not only by major commitments such as schooling, but by the steady accumulation of ordinary needs - meals, groceries, clothes, transport, and all the little things that rarely feel significant until they are added together.

For many families, spending more on their children means finding somewhere else to cut back. The survey found that reducing personal spending was the most common adjustment parents had made, cited by 30% of respondents.
Another 22% had scaled back lifestyle spending, while 16% postponed major purchases and 11% sought additional income. Only 9% said becoming a parent had not required any financial adjustment.
In practical terms, those compromises may mean fewer meals out, putting off a new phone or holiday, or simply becoming more careful about purchases that once required little thought.
These are often modest sacrifices individually, but together they reveal how family priorities shift once children enter the picture.

Yet even as day-to-day costs prove higher than expected, many parents are still trying to protect their children’s longer-term future. Some 78% of respondents said they already had savings or investments set aside specifically for their children, while most of those who had not started said they intended to do so.
There is something revealing in that contrast: even when today’s household budget is under pressure, saving for tomorrow remains difficult for many parents to abandon.
Before having children, it is tempting to think family finances can be neatly mapped out - childcare, education, healthcare, savings and perhaps the occasional family holiday.

In reality, children have a way of making spreadsheets look optimistic. They grow out of shoes and clothes, appetites change, school expenses appear, and unexpected medical or household costs can upset even a carefully planned month.

That does not necessarily mean parents underestimate the responsibility of having children. Rather, it shows how difficult it is to anticipate the cumulative cost of needs that evolve over many years.
The survey involved 677 parents among 2,565 Malaysians polled through an app, so its results should not be taken as representative of all Malaysian families.
Still, the findings reflect a dilemma that will feel familiar to many households: how to give children a good life today without neglecting what they may need tomorrow.
653144da3f9afc34: From Terence Netto
Hassan Karim's opinion that the conditional pardon for Najib Razak is a “golden opportunity” for Pakatan Harapan, deserves attention – and, more pointedly, exploitation.

Since last November, PH and its component parties have been reeling from electoral setbacks in Sabah, Johor and Negeri Sembilan. Rubbing salt into the wound was the glee displayed by its erstwhile partner Umno over the PH defeats.

It was particularly galling in Negeri Sembilan, where the PKR-led state government was toppled and DAP’s Loke Siew Fook defeated at the hands of an MCA opponent who was cheered on by none other than Umno chief Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
The fact that Zahid sits next to Loke in the Cabinet did not give the Umno president pause in his quest of electoral spoils. Apparently, all is fair and foul in Cabinet and on the hustings.
If Zahid lacks esprit de corps, PH need not bother about decorum in seeking to exploit Najib’s conditional pardon for electoral advantage.
Equality under the law

However one looks at the pardon and the house arrest arrangement for Najib, it sits ill with ordinary people, who are apt to think that there is one rule for the super-elite and another for the hoi polloi.
This is despite the fact that many people think Najib was a good prime minister, especially during the first 18 months after he took over from Abdullah Ahmad Badawi in 2009.
Nothing grates more on ordinary people’s sense of being underprivileged than seeing the guarantee of equal treatment before the law honoured more in the breach than in the observance.
Also, Umno’s decision to organise a fundraiser for Najib to pay his RM50 million fine in order to fulfil a condition of his house arrest must rank as a faux pas of disastrous proportions.
It is like asking victims to help pay the fine imposed on a felon caught with his hands in the public till.
Public morality

Because the issue of Najib Razak and his responsibility for the financial scandals arising from the 1MDB imbroglio involves questions of public morality and accountability, it is heartening to hear what Amanah deputy president Mujahid Yusof Rawa has said.
Amanah has not particularly distinguished itself in handling these issues because of the space it has conceded to PAS and its president, Abdul Hadi Awang, who have ruled the rhetorical roost.

At any one time, it is difficult to sort out what the PAS supremo is actually saying because his writings and speeches are clouded in jargon. Listeners give up, if for no other reason than that the subject matter has to do with Islam, a subject about which a non-Muslim, especially, must tread with caution.

So, when Mujahid, in criticising Umno and PAS for celebrating the grant of a conditional pardon to Najib, spoke of the tawdriness of the moral compass of both parties, he employed a clarity that was the reverse of Hadi’s opacity.
“What has happened to the moral compass of our Malay people?” Mujahid said.

“It’s time the Malays made an important decision for the sake of their dignity. Don’t allow Malay dignity to be represented by those who normalise crime, otherwise our future generations will consider corruption as heroics for the Malay people,” the Amanah leader said plaintively.
PH has been on the back foot for some years now, a consequence of Anwar Ibrahim’s strange loss of effectiveness and clarity of vision.
The “golden opportunity” presented by Najib’s conditional pardon and Umno’s fundraising are a shot in the foot by Umno and PAS that PH must exploit to the hilt.
A gift horse is not to be looked at in the mouth.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

56b7ee26f9ef2977: BOGOTA: Colombia's president on Sunday denied having a "policy of revenge" against a special peace tribunal that administers justice for the worst crimes of Colombia's decades-long armed civil conflict.

A pro-government senator on Thursday introduced a bill to reduce the state budget allocated to the tribunal by around US$31 million - a proposal supported by president Abelardo de la Espriella, who has promised to use force against rebels, and has argued that the court has been too lenient on them.

"I do not have a policy of revenge against the JEP," De la Espriella said on X, using a Spanish acronym for the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, which was created under a landmark peace deal with the now-defunct rebel army FARC in 2016.

"I have a duty to bring order to spending, demand results, and allocate the State's limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a tribunal that a segment of the country perceives...as a system of benefits," he added.
Under the proposed bill, the savings from cutting the tribunal's budget from US$230 million to US$199 million would go toward the traditional justice system.
The tribunal's president Alejandro Ramelli on Friday likened the budget cut to "economic asphyxiation."

The tribunal, which issued its first verdicts last year, hands down alternative sentences to prison time as part of broader efforts to achieve a lasting peace after a conflict that claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
In one ruling, senior FARC leaders were sentenced to eight years of community service, as well as having their movements restricted, after carrying out over 21,000 kidnappings.
Twelve retired military officers responsible for the disappearance and extrajudicial execution of civilians received similar sentences.
23c206cc0d0bd21e: PORT AU PRINCE: A military plane whisked 18 suspects in the 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moise out of Haiti and flew them to the United States on Sunday, according to Jason Reding Quinones, the US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida.
"Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination," Quinones said in a statement posted on social media.

The 53-year-old president was shot dead in July 2021 at his private residence in the hills ​above Port-au-Prince, a killing that left a gaping political vacuum in the Caribbean nation and emboldened powerful armed groups in the country.
The killing ​has prompted multiple investigations and indictments in Haiti and the US.
On Sunday, Haitian justice minister Patrick Pelissier confirmed in a statement that suspects had been transferred from Haiti to the US, adding that Haitian judicial proceedings had been delayed.

"While the American procedure has recorded significant progress, notably arrests, prosecutions, and convictions, the Haitian procedure remains confronted with major difficulties and has not, to date, resulted in a trial being held, after five years of proceedings."

US prosecutors have argued that suspects in the case used South Florida as a "staging ground for a deadly foreign plot." Thirty people have been indicted in the US in relation to the crime, according to Quinones' statement on Sunday.
In May, four South Florida men were convicted of plotting to kill the Haitian president by hiring mercenaries to ​assassinate him at his Port-au-Prince home.

Prosecutors argued during the nine-week trial in a ‌Miami federal court that the men assembled two dozen former Colombian soldiers and supplied them with money, guns, ammunition and tactical vests in a conspiracy to kill Moise.
In Haiti, prominent human rights activist Pierre Esperance said that the slow pace of the Haitian case and the transfer of the 18 suspects to the US was a "disgrace for the Haitian justice system".
He argued for strengthening the country's justice system to allow for such complex cases to be tried inside Haiti, rather than sending them to the US for prosecution.
7639aa2efecd5876: MANCHESTER: Manchester City will enjoy a three-point Premier League lead for the next three weeks after Arsenal's perfect start came off the rails in a 3-0 defeat at Brighton.
City conceded three times themselves to Sunderland's Brian Brobbey but had enough firepower of their own to beat the Black Cats 5-3.
Chelsea were also defeated 3-0 at Brentford to take the shine off Xabi Alonso's start at Stamford Bridge, while Manchester United could only manage a 1-1 draw at winless Fulham.
AFP Sport looks at three talking points from the Premier League weekend:
Arsenal aura undone
The champions had been tipped to romp to the title after another summer of smart recruitment and a dominant start to the campaign.
But Brighton showed the rest of the Premier League that the Gunners do have flaws by inflicting their heaviest defeat in over three years.
Mikel Arteta's men arrived on the south-coast in formidable form having won all seven games in all competitions this season.
Arsenal, though, struggled to cope with the Seagulls' high press and were even uncharacteristically exposed defensively from a corner when Chema Andres headed in Brighton's third.
"The way we have competed, the way we have played, the way we have dominated. It's been really good," said Arteta on his side's start to the season.
"But today we need to take this lesson very, very seriously because it's going to happen."
Carrick defiant as Man Utd feel heat

Assailed by stinging criticism of Manchester United's abject performance in their 1-1 draw against lowly Fulham on Sunday, Michael Carrick mounted an unconvincing defence of his spluttering side as the pressure mounted.
United have won just once in five league games, equalling their worst start to the season in the Premier League era.
It would have been even worse for Carrick but for Matheus Cunha's last-gasp equaliser at Craven Cottage.

United trailed to a farcical second half goal that summed up their malaise as Lisandro Martinez made a hash of clearing from Senne Lammens's save and scuffed the ball into his own net via a deflection off his keeper.

Giving away possession carelessly time and again, while lacking the basic defensive solidity to contain a previously moribund Fulham attack, United looked no better than the lethargic group that struggled under Carrick's predecessor Ruben Amorim.
Carrick proved a stabilising force after replacing the sacked Amorim last season but the positives vibes created by that third-place finish are quickly fading.
Piling on the misery for Carrick, his former team-mate Gary Neville issued a damning indictment.
"I've watched Man United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," said Neville of United's start to the second half.
"Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must Carrick be thinking?"
Chelsea 'bullied' by Brentford
The dazzling start made by Chelsea's front three of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers papered over the cracks of the Blues' defensive problems.
Chelsea have now gone three games without a win as their inability to keep a clean sheet goes on.
It is now 21 league games since they did not concede, the club's longest run since 1965.
That run predates Alonso's time in charge, but he knows a major change is needed after becoming only the sixth manager to concede at least twice in his first five Premier League games.
"Not good enough," said Chelsea defender Levi Colwill. "At times we have been bullied in the box and we definitely need to improve."
1e5c6baf9a65723c: KOTA BHARU, Sept 21 — The influence of partners, be it husbands or boyfriends, is the main reason for the increase in the number of drug addicts among women in Kelantan last year, with 598 cases compared with 526 the previous year.

National Anti-Drugs Agency (AADK) director-general Datuk Ruslin Jusoh said a study found that life stress was the main factor acknowledged by all respondents, with most cases stemming from marital conflicts and husbands’ behaviour that frequently triggered problems.
“This situation pushes women to use drugs as a coping mechanism to forget their anxiety and emotional pain caused by their partners,” he told Bernama recently.
Ruslin said that apart from emotional stress, women were also often subjected to psychological manipulation by partners who normalised drug use on the grounds of enhancing beauty and productivity.

“They were also influenced by those closest to them to believe that stimulant-type drugs could help with weight management, flatten the stomach after childbirth and provide extra energy to complete household chores faster.

“The reality on the ground shows that women’s involvement in drug abuse in the state rarely occurs in isolation; on the contrary, the risk of involvement becomes significantly higher when they live in a family environment where a member, particularly a husband, is also a drug user,” he said.

He said this cycle was made worse by factors such as neglect and loneliness, especially following divorce or a breakdown in relationships, which caused women to seek temporary solace through illicit substances.

“Amphetamine-Type Stimulants (ATS) were the most widely used illicit substances among women in Kelantan last year, with 557 people, while those aged 19 to 39 recorded the highest number of drug abuse cases, involving 409 individuals.
“In conclusion, drug addiction among women in Kelantan is often a manifestation of interpersonal stress and manipulation by partners in an unhealthy domestic ecosystem,” he said.

He said AADK also measured the effectiveness and achievements of its Community-Based Treatment and Rehabilitation (RPDK) programme based on the Client Recovery Index (IKK), with female clients in Kelantan recording an achievement rate of 76.4 per cent last year.

“Of the 55 female clients assessed, 42 achieved a level of recovery in the good and excellent categories. This figure reflects the effectiveness of the recovery centre’s support and the active involvement of families in helping female clients maintain their recovery in the community,” he added. — Bernama
dad5c712748cf813: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 21 — Nasi kandar with mixed curry gravies, fried cabbage and honey chicken paired with teh tarik are no longer impossible to enjoy in Phu Quoc, Vietnam’s largest island, which is increasingly attracting Malaysian tourists.
Mina Nasi Kandar Halal, situated in the island’s main town, is run by businessman Dr Nash Ramesh, 52, and a friend from Langkawi, Kedah.
They started the restaurant nearly three months ago after recognising the potential for a halal restaurant based on their own experiences holidaying there.

“After spending three days in Phu Quoc, we felt that the food options were rather limited, although there were several halal restaurants. So, we wanted to provide an alternative to tourists, especially those from Malaysia or who have previously visited our country and experienced Malaysian cuisine.
“As a Malaysian and someone with a Muslim business partner, I understand how important halal requirements are to Muslim tourists,” he said when met at his restaurant recently.

He said the chicken and meat used at the restaurant are purchased exclusively from Halal Mart, a member of Halal Vietnam that is recognised by the Department of Islamic Development Malaysia (Jakim), adding that the relevant authorities also conduct inspections almost every month to ensure compliance with halal certification requirements.

Nash, who hails from Taiping, Perak, said dry ingredients, particularly spices, are not a problem because he owns a logistics business in Ho Chi Minh City and is the sole distributor in Vietnam for a popular Malaysian spice brand.

“However, I still go back to Malaysia every few months to purchase items that are difficult to get here, such as belacan (shrimp paste), because we also prepare dishes using this ingredient, including sambal belacan served with ulam (vegetables) such as cucumber and salad, as well as boiled okra,” he said.

Nash said the restaurant, which began operations on July 28, is the first Malaysian restaurant in Phu Quoc and the first nasi kandar restaurant in Vietnam, adding that it has received a very positive response not only from Malaysian tourists, but also visitors from Brunei, Singapore, India, China and Arab countries.

Asked whether the food served at the restaurant tastes authentic like Malaysian cuisine, Nash said he brought with him four chefs from Malaysia, while his 37-year-old wife Van Anh, a Vietnamese national, has also learned various Malaysian recipes since they married 15 years ago.

The restaurant, which has 11 employees, also offers popular Vietnamese food such as pho and banh mi, as well as nasi lemak, fried noodles and roti canai as part of its breakfast buffet when catering to groups of tourists.

“We have also received a good response from the locals, especially for the roti canai, which is prepared in front of customers and sold from 30,000 Vietnamese dong (about RM4), with more people also becoming familiar with nasi kandar because they had visited Malaysia.

“For the selection of dishes, popular choices include ayam kicap (soy sauce chicken), honey chicken and ayam berempah (spiced chicken), while our speciality is daging kicap (soy sauce beef), and teh tarik, teh O, Nescafe and iced lime drinks are often the preferred choice of beverage.

“If customers request a particular dish or drink, we will do our best to fulfil their requests as long as the ingredients are readily available here,” said Nash, who also offers an a la carte menu featuring a variety of hot dishes starting from 85,000 Vietnamese dong (about RM13).
The restaurant, which operates daily from 8am to 10pm, also has a surau because the majority of its customers are Muslim.

“This restaurant also helps ease my longing to meet and chat with Malaysians, as more and more of them are choosing to holiday in Phu Quoc, especially as the halal restaurant scene here continues to grow,” said Nash, who has been living in Vietnam for the past 12 years. — Bernama
94c97fd6cbf0e2e2: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 21 — E-sports enthusiast and full-time accountant Mohamed Ilyas Suhairi returns to video games to unwind after a long day, as there is always something new to explore.
The 26-year-old said he was drawn to e-sports because it allowed him to relax, have fun and connect with friends.
“When I started following e-sports, I became interested in watching how players compete, how teams play differently and how the games can become so intense,” he told Bernama recently.

Mohamed Ilyas said his passion for the sport is reflected in the several gaming gadgets he owns, including a gaming computer, a PlayStation 5, a Nintendo Switch and several handheld consoles, which give him different ways to enjoy games depending on his mood and interests.

What began as an interest in playing games eventually led Mohamed Ilyas to follow tournaments and the wider e-sports scene, giving him a closer look at how gaming has grown from a leisure activity into a professional industry.
In Malaysia’s expanding e-sports ecosystem, professional tournaments attract large audiences, garner commercial partnerships, and create opportunities throughout the broader digital economy.
From being casual gamers, many have gone on to pursue careers in e-sports, such as professional players, content creators, streamers, analysts, and many more.
E-sports as part of the digital economy

Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation (MDEC) chief executive officer Anuar Fariz Fadzil said e-sports is an integral part of Malaysia’s broader digital content ecosystem and has evolved into an industry that creates economic opportunities far beyond professional competition.

“E-sports falls under the bigger digital content initiative. We have animation, we have games, we have e-sports. These initiatives give children, sportsmen and athletes an opportunity in life. This is considered a way to make a living and is even recognised on the global stage,” he told Bernama.
Anuar Fariz said the industry’s value lies not only in producing professional players but also in developing a wider talent pool and creating digital jobs across various disciplines.
“In e-sports, we have a broader talent pool, not just players. We have coaches, we have the production teams, we have the animators,” he said.

Anuar Fariz said MDEC remains focused on creating more digital jobs and strengthening the country’s digital talent pipeline through initiatives including grants, talent development and industry engagement.
According to the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO), the video game industry generated an estimated revenue of US$184 billion in 2023.
It said China leads in e-sports revenues, followed by the United States, with regional distribution showing Asia-Pacific dominating with 46 per cent of the market.

According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA), gaming is part of the country’s creative-industry ecosystem and requires highly skilled professionals in graphic material digitisation, digital sound, character programming and creative-content creation.
Malaysian institutions offer courses in game software development, game art and design and game programming.
Malaysia’s digital economy contributed 25.5 per cent to the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025, with the government targeting a 30 per cent contribution by 2030.
From gaming communities to world-class events

Recognising the potential, Malaysia has actively supported the e-sports ecosystem, and this is also reflected in the emergence of professional tournament organisers capable of staging major international competitions and reaching audiences around the world.

Among them is IO Esports, which has established itself as one of Malaysia’s prominent e-sports event organisers through its involvement in major competitions, including the Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (MLBB) Professional League (MPL) Malaysia and the M6 World Championship.

The M6 World Championship, held in Kuala Lumpur in 2024, recorded more than 4.1 million peak concurrent viewers and over 85 million hours watched, making it the most-watched M Series tournament at the time.

Moonton Games, the developer and publisher of MLBB, reported that the event generated more than 115 million euros in brand value, underlining the commercial potential of large-scale e-sports tournaments.
The strength of the e-sports audience is evident across regular leagues and regional tournaments, rather than being confined to major world championships.

MPL Malaysia Season 18 has so far accumulated 7.22 million hours watched and reached a peak concurrent viewership of 391,947, highlighting the sustained audience interest in Malaysia’s premier domestic e-sports league.

The recently concluded PUBG Mobile Global Open 2026 Season 2 Southeast Asia Finals recorded 2.98 million hours watched and a peak of 538,624 viewers, while the ongoing MY Honor of Kings League Fall 2026 has recorded 26,395 hours watched and a peak of 5,067 viewers so far.

MPL Malaysia has demonstrated the depth of the domestic audience, with Season 14 in 2024 recording a league-record peak of 870,049 concurrent viewers, the highest in the league’s history and more than 13.14 million hours watched.

Malaysia has also hosted several other major international e-sports events, including ESL One Genting, the PUBG Global Series, the M1 World Championship and the IESF World E-sports Championship, reinforcing its position as one of Southeast Asia’s leading e-sports destinations.
Is there enough funding to support the growth?

Under Budget 2025, the government allocated RM20 million to strengthen the e-sports ecosystem, including talent development and the upgrading of e-sports arenas. Of that amount, RM10 million was earmarked for the construction of a dedicated e-sports stadium, with the remainder for training and other e-sports activities.
The industry’s development has also been accompanied by government support, from grassroots participation to high-performance and international competition.

The scale of grassroots interest is also reflected in the Malaysia E-sports League (MEL), which recorded more than 62,000 participants across five editions from 2021 to 2025, according to the Ministry of Youth and Sports.
From 2023 to 2025, the government approved 406 e-sports-related applications involving tournaments, talent development and digital content, with total allocations of RM13.23 million.

Beyond e-sports-specific initiatives, MDEC has also strengthened the broader games and digital creative ecosystem, launching the Digital Games Testbed Programme in April 2025 with RM3.5 million in funding for at least five Malaysian game development companies.
Each of these companies is eligible for up to RM700,000 to develop new game genres, strengthen local intellectual property and pursue international partnerships.

Meanwhile, MIDA also highlighted initiatives such as MDEC’s LEVEL UP KL in supporting the development of Malaysia’s games industry, which has grown into a regional platform connecting game developers, publishers, investors, service providers and other industry players through its industry conference, business connection programme, exhibition and pitching activities.

While the initiatives indicate growing attention to e-sports and the wider games industry, the rapid expansion of audiences, talent and commercial opportunities also raises the question of whether continued investment can keep pace with the sector’s development and support Malaysia’s ambitions to compete at the regional and global levels.
Wider business ecosystem

The industry’s growth has also created new career paths for former professional players, with some transitioning into streaming and content creation on platforms such as TikTok and YouTube while leveraging their personal brands and established fan bases.

Beyond streaming income, former players can monetise their audiences through viewer donations, sponsorships, paid content and merchandise sales, creating alternative income streams after their competitive careers.

SociaBuzz, a creator-support platform widely used by Malaysian streamers, citing Malaysia-based digital studio Miura Visual, said independent gaming creators in Malaysia typically earn up to RM2,000 a month, while mid-level creators can earn as much as RM10,000 a month, although actual earnings vary considerably based on audience size and engagement.

The wider digital content industry also illustrates the commercial potential surrounding gaming and related creative sectors, with MDEC reporting RM87.25 billion in revenue and RM11.18 billion in export sales, while creating employment for some 11,154 Malaysians since 2011.

The growth of e-sports has also attracted partnerships between global and local brands and Malaysian e-sports organisations, with companies such as Red Bull, Infinix, Sony, U Mobile and CelcomDigi sponsoring professional teams, tournaments and digital content initiatives, reflecting its increasing commercial value.

As Malaysia accelerates its digital economy ambitions, e-sports is increasingly being positioned not merely as entertainment, but as part of a wider digital ecosystem capable of supporting talent development, innovation, digital employment and economic activity.
The question now is whether Malaysia can sustain this momentum and turn its growing e-sports audience and talent into lasting opportunities across the digital economy. — Bernama
e7c241cd41e2e562: SINGAPORE, Sept 21 — A steady nerve is crucial when keeping watch over hundreds of data centres worldwide, facilities essential to the frictionless online banking, messaging and AI services that society relies on.
Analysts sit surrounded by digital maps and dashboards at the Singapore command centre of US firm Digital Realty, a major global operator of the warehouse-like sites filled with whirring servers.
The goal is not simply to react when something breaks, but to detect warning signs, such as a sudden rise in temperature, early enough to prevent disruption.
Daniel Naing, 37, and his colleagues handle thousands of system alerts flagging signs of trouble each week.
“If I panic, my team members will panic. So even though inside I may be nervous, I cannot show it,” he told AFP.
The command centre and its two sister hubs, in Europe and the United States, provide round-the-clock oversight of more than 300 data centres across six continents.
Digital Realty rents its server space to around 6,000 companies big and small, with power disruptions and equipment failure the most common issues faced.
There are also detailed protocols for earthquakes and typhoons, and an approaching storm thousands of kilometres away is enough to put the team on standby.
Booming demand for data centres is a political hot potato in many places, as tech companies race to develop artificial intelligence tools that require massive amounts of computing power.
But without them “nothing works” in our high-tech world, said Serene Nah, managing director and head of Asia Pacific at Digital Realty.
Data centres are essential infrastructure — a matter “almost like national security”, she said.
“We need to be up running all the time.”
Nah said, however, that “our business is very misunderstood” and has little support from the public, who believe data centres emit “a lot of carbon or heat” or “use up a lot of water”.
“Yet everyone’s scrolling their phones every day,” and for each swipe “the data needs to go somewhere”.
The company is prioritising renewable energy such as solar panels and closed-loop server cooling systems that continuously recycle water, Nah said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The data centre is prioritising renewable energy such as solar panels and closed-loop server cooling systems that continuously recycle water. — AFP pic
False positives
The vulnerabilities of the sector were highlighted this year, when data centres run by Amazon’s cloud arm were struck during the Middle East war.
Data centres operate 24 hours a day, so Naing and his colleagues take the 7am to 7pm shift in Singapore before handing over to Europe.
Engineers must attend to an alert within minutes. The teams liaise with those on the ground and call on a global network of experts to help, while keeping clients updated.
Digital Realty is one of the biggest providers of data centre server space along with rivals like Equinix, also a US company.
Meanwhile tech giants from Microsoft to Alibaba are racing to build their own data centres to train and run AI models — part of a global buildout costing trillions of dollars.
Digital Realty’s Global Command Centre in Singapore is housed inside one of three data centres that the company runs in the city-state.
Most areas of the data centre, whose roof is lined with solar panels, are off-limits for security reasons.

But AFP was shown a room where rows of black server cabinets formed long, narrow corridors, with bundles of yellow cables running overhead and the computer servers’ high-velocity fans emitting a soft hum.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on September 2, 2026 shows rows of server rack cabinets at the Digital Realty data centre in Singapore. — AFP pic
AI is accelerating the growth and complexity of data centres, but for operations at the command centre, humans remain indispensable, said Terence Tang, head of the Asia Pacific global command centre.

“We still need human intervention to really look at whether or not those are genuine outages, genuine alerts and alarms, because sometimes AI or automation can give you false positives,” Tang told AFP. — AFP
59086a6155fa5379: VATICAN CITY, Sept 21 — Papal trips mean vast crowds, high-level diplomatic meetings and a formidable amount of behind-the-scenes preparation, from delicately balanced agendas to complex security protection for the head of the Catholic Church.
Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France from September 25 to 28, which includes events at the Notre-Dame Cathedral and the Champs-Elysees, will involve some 15,000 members of the security forces.
The groundwork for this visit — the first papal trip to Paris since 2008 — was laid well before it was officially announced.
Countries invite the pope, but whether or not he visits is based on a range of pastoral and political considerations.
The complex decision “depends heavily on the international context”, a Vatican source told AFP.
The Vatican takes into account social and political circumstances, from conflicts to humanitarian crises, as well as the situation of the local church and the history of previous visits.
But each pope has his own wish list and the choice of destinations also reflects the papacy’s geopolitical priorities.
For example, “John Paul II travelled extensively to eastern European countries to denounce Communism,” the source said.

In his 12 years as pontiff, the Argentinian Pope Francis favoured the “peripheries” of the Church, from Iraq to Mongolia and Papua New Guinea, while US-born Leo seems more inclined towards Europe and major international institutions.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A marquee is set up at Place de la Concorde ahead of Pope Leo XIV’s France visit. — AFP pic
Sky-high briefing

Since the Vatican does not have an official aircraft, the Holy See charters a commercial plane from Italian national airline ITA for the outbound journey, while the return flight is generally operated by the host country.
On board, the pope occupies seat 1A, at the front left of the cabin. In front of him is a depiction of the Virgin Mary.
Beside him, in seats bearing the Holy See coat of arms, sit cardinals, his private secretaries, and a doctor.
Dressed in dark suits and ties, some 40 officers from the Vatican Gendarmerie and Swiss Guard provide close protection.
In the rear of the cabin travel the media: approximately 80 journalists, photographers and cameramen.
Media outlets pay for their correspondents’ tickets, which generally cost several thousand euros.
On the outbound journey, the pope walks down the plane, greeting the journalists individually.
He sometimes shares a few personal anecdotes and some correspondents give him presents — from football shirts to food.
On the return trip, the pontiff holds one of the most closely watched press conferences in the world: a sky-high briefing at 10,000 metres in a cabin cluttered with cameras, microphones and tripods.
The luggage includes the pope’s personal belongings, speeches prepared weeks in advance, and security equipment.

There are also sealed cases containing liturgical objects — such as chasubles, to be worn during mass — and dozens of official gifts for heads of state and dignitaries, such as paintings, books or rosaries.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Pope Leo XIV waves to the crowd from the pope-mobile as he arrives to lead the Holy Mass in Douala on the fifth day of an 11-day apostolic journey to Africa, on April 17, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Advance team’
Security and logistics are the biggest challenges. With his dual status as head of state and leader of 1.4 billion Catholics, the pope is one of the most heavily protected figures in the world.
The medical team carries a supply of the pope’s blood type, while a hospital suite is kept on standby in the host country.
The iconic white pope-mobile is transported in advance and a backup vehicle is ready on site.
Journalists including AFP precede the pope at every stage in a convoy escorted by law enforcement, with sirens blaring.
As before each trip, a Vatican delegation known as the “advance team” travelled to France in mid-July to finalise the details with local authorities.
“The programme can change at the very last minute,” a Vatican security source told AFP.
“Everything has to be meticulously planned, almost down to the second.” — AFP
6563681e21fb3442: In January, US president Donald Trump suggested that his newly created Board of Peace might eventually replace the United Nations. It’s easy to dismiss this as Trump’s typical bluster, but it also underscores the UN’s loss of credibility.
The problem is that the world still desperately needs an institution capable of bringing countries together to tackle global challenges like climate change.

Amid escalating geopolitical rivalries, Security Council paralysis, funding cuts, and the growing willingness of countries like the US to disengage from multilateral institutions, almost every UN mandate is under strain.
Whoever succeeds António Guterres as secretary-general in January will need to work with member states to restore confidence in the UN’s ability to act and show that multilateralism can still work.
The UN remains the closest thing the world has to a universal forum. Its legitimacy rests on the scope of its membership. But legitimacy does not guarantee credibility.

To prove itself worthy of the role the world needs it to play, the UN must demonstrate that multilateral processes can be transparent, that commitments can be enforced, and that those who make the rules can be held accountable.

This credibility test begins with the process for choosing the next secretary-general. While candidates vying to replace Guterres have published detailed vision statements and faced questions from civil-society groups, the decision remains largely opaque, with the Security Council’s five permanent members wielding outsize influence.

The irony is striking: the UN is asking the world to trust multilateral institutions, yet its most important appointment is decided behind closed doors. How leaders are chosen affects their credibility once in office, making it essential that the process itself be free of conflicts of interest.

The same applies to collective negotiations. While the 2015 Paris climate agreement remains the broadest pact the UN has ever brokered, its largely non-binding structure has left implementation dependent on governments’ willingness to follow through on their pledges.

A decade later, that willingness has been no match for the industries working to impede climate action. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) still lacks clear, system-wide rules for identifying and managing conflicts of interest, and fossil-fuel interests continue to influence climate negotiations with little scrutiny.

Research by Transparency International found that more than half of the participants at last year’s UN Climate Change Conference (COP30) in Belém did not fully disclose their institutional affiliations.

Guterres has used his tenure to push for climate action, criticising the fossil-fuel industry for expanding production despite knowing that its business model was incompatible with human survival, and has called for a windfall tax on oil and gas profits. But even that is not enough.

With the UN Environment Programme warning that, at the current rate, the global-warming threshold of 1.5° Celsius will be breached within three years, the stakes are too high not to know who shapes the world’s response—and to what end.

The next secretary-general won’t have the authority to set conflict-of-interest rules for the UNFCCC process; such rules are for governments to negotiate and adopt. But that does not mean the secretary-general is powerless.

The position’s public platform and influence across the UN system could be used to press governments and COP presidencies for tougher integrity standards, thereby making it clear that the credibility of the UN’s climate efforts depends on the credibility of those given a seat at the negotiating table.

Collective action is also needed to tackle high-level corruption, state capture, and the global networks that conceal illicit wealth. International rules are only as effective as the governments willing to implement them and the institutions enforcing them. Both sets of actors can be compromised by the very interests they’re supposed to regulate.
The UN Convention against Corruption remains one of the most important global frameworks for setting common standards and holding governments to them.

The next phase of its review in Vienna, which will focus on criminalisation and enforcement, offers a unique opportunity to bolster its accountability mechanisms. But for it to succeed, governments must allow their own records to be scrutinised.

These are not separate problems. Whether it is fossil-fuel interests compromising the COP process, the UN’s corruption framework going unenforced, or the Security Council being paralysed by great-power interests, the question is the same: Does multilateralism still have teeth, or can governments ignore its rules without consequence?

The next secretary-general cannot answer that question alone. But they can decide to spend their political capital on making transparency a top priority, pushing conflicts of interest into the open before they become scandals, and pressuring governments to keep their promises.

History offers plenty of precedents. From Dag Hammarskjöld to Kofi A Annan, secretaries-general have repeatedly exercised influence well beyond their formal mandates by building political credibility and personal authority.

While candidates in this round have spoken about efficiency, preventive diplomacy, and restoring confidence in the UN, they have said far less about how they would ensure transparency and hold member states to account.

To rebuild credibility, the UN must start from within. That means greater openness about how decisions are made, how resources are used, and how commitments are implemented. With trust in multilateralism already in decline, the UN must hold itself to the same standards it expects of others.
Maíra Martini is CEO of Transparency International.
