9bcbb90e0a7d76bc: Di Malaysia sekarang, dunia dah terbalik. Mereka yang bermuka-muka dengan musuh politik tetapi masih enjoy jadi menteri, macam tak ada malu langsung. Lepas itu, mereka juga yang menyokong penyakau wang rakyat tetapi tak kisah nak letak jawatan pun. Namun demikian, ada yang berhempas pulas menentang sakauan duit rakyat, dihina sebagai ejen penjajah, sebagai musuh Islam; nampaknya mereka ini pula yang ada maruah dan integriti serta sanggup meletak jawatan.

Jadi, saya amat memuji tindakan kepimpinan DAP, saudara Loke Siew Fook yang sanggup mengorbankan jawatannya demi mempertahankan nilai serta integriti partinya yang menentang sesiapa yang merompak duit kepunyaan semua rakyat Malaysia. Saya jangka bahawa Loke akan berkeras untuk meletak jawatan walaupun nanti dipujuk supaya jangan oleh Anwar Ibrahim. Loke memilih untuk mengambil jalan sebagai kapten kapal yang mengambil tanggungjawab tertinggi sekali. Ini baru peletakan jawatan yang bertanggungjawab, berintegriti dan berstrategik. Bukan peletakan ada satu dua bekas menteri yang merajuk kalah jawatan parti. Bukan juga olok-olokan hulubalang Melaka yang kata nak berhenti tetapi sampai hari ini pun haram tak berhenti.

Loke adalah pemimpin yang saya cukup hormati. Seketika 2022, November di mana negara hampir jatuh ke tangan Perikatan Nasional, Loke telah dengan sendirinya terbang ke Kuching berjumpa terus dengan Abang Jo, seteru DAP di Sarawak untuk berdamai. Langkah ini adalah suatu pengorbanan ego yang besar demi menyelamatkan Malaysia dari jatuh ke tangan parti politik perkauman.

Saya juga masih ingat kata-kata Loke bahawa DAP menawarkan untuk tidak menyertai Kabinet secara langsung kerana takut Umno tidak bersetuju untuk bekerjasama dalam kerajaan perpaduan yang dicadangkan Agong. Ini suatu pengorbanan besar jika ia berlaku tetapi tidak sedemikian dan Umno bekerjasama dengan DAP sambil membiarkan Dr Akmal Saleh menyalak di luar menghina parti kawan itu. Biasalah, taktik Umno.

DAP, kini, dalam kes pengampunan bersyarat Najib Razak bakal menjadi hero atau perwira yang menyelamatkan Pakatan Harapan di PRU16 nanti. Loke menjelaskan bahawa kepimpinan DAP mengambil keputusan untuk tidak keluar semua daripada Kabinet kerajaan perpaduan supaya menjaga kestabilan politiknya.

DAP tidak mahu memberi peluang kepada musuh-musuh dalam dan luar menggunakan kekosongan Kabinet untuk peluru-peluru mereka. Maka itu Loke mencadangkan bahawa hanya beliau sahaja menjadi simbol yang terkilan atas pengampunan bersyarat Najib walaupun menghormati keputusan Agong. Walaupun ramai ahli Kabinet lain yang menawarkan diri untuk meletak jawatan, namun Loke berkeras supaya beliau seorang sahaja yang resign. Hebat. A real leader.

Keputusan ini sekali gus akan melenyapkan kata-kata sinis dan perli-perli geng Umno, PAS dan PN serta Barisan Nasional yang menyinggung isu peletakan jawatan kerana Nga Kor Ming yang membuat kenyataan tersebut.

Keputusan ini juga akan menjadi rangsangan kepada penyokong-penyokong DAP yang sebelum ini ada yang agak tawar hati dengan parti itu sehinggakan memberi protest vote kepada MCA. Sekarang, siapa yang lebih matang dan berani? Keputusan Loke juga akan memberi suatu persepsi kekaguman kepada pengundi-pengundi atas pagar yang juga terkilan dengan keputusan pengampunan bersyarat ini. Apatah lagi bila melihat rumah Najib yang sebesar istana yang mungkin bakal dihuninya selama dua tahun lagi.

Syabas sekali lagi saya ucapkan kepada saudara Loke. I am sorry to see you go as a good performing minister. Namun demikian, sebagai pemimpin, pengorbanan sedemikian adalah yang paling nyata, terbaik dan bermakna bukan sahaja kepada parti sendiri tetapi juga kepada orang tua seperti saya, rakyat Malaysia yang biasa. Saya berasa amat bertuah mengenali seorang pemimpin rakyat Malaysia yang berwibawa, profesional dan berintegriti sebagai pemimpin anak cucu saya di Malaysia kini dan masa depan.
Syabas, Loke, way to go, sir.

1a31c8f28bcdb297: PETALING JAYA: This year’s haze has affected large parts of the country, and its worsening in recent days has made it increasingly difficult to ignore.

A state of emergency was declared on Sept 4 when the Air Pollutant Index (API) in Serian, Sarawak, surpassed 500. By Sept 15, unhealthy air quality had been recorded at 40 of Malaysia’s 68 monitoring stations nationwide, up from 23 the previous day.

Eventually, the skies will clear and life will return to normal, with recent rains already bringing a welcome respite to places such as the Klang Valley. But while the haze may disappear from sight, experts warn that the effects of repeatedly breathing polluted air may not be so temporary.

For Dr Anand Sachithanandan, president of Lung Cancer Network Malaysia (LCNM) and a cardiothoracic surgeon, the bigger concern is not simply what Malaysians breathe during a single haze episode, but the cumulative exposure from experiencing it year after year.

“Chronic and cumulative exposure to the ‘annual’ transboundary regional haze, like what Malaysians have been exposed to over the past decade, will certainly elevate the risk of future lung cancer,” he warned.
LCNM recently highlighted the issue at the 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer in Seoul, warning that the annual transboundary haze should be regarded as a significant long-term health hazard.

A major concern is PM2.5, microscopic particles measuring 2.5 micrometres or less that can penetrate deep into the lungs. According to Anand, repeated exposure can cause chronic inflammation, potentially contributing to respiratory disease and activating dormant cancer-causing genes in genetically susceptible individuals.
“Over the years, my colleagues and I have observed and treated increasingly more cases of lung cancer in non-smokers and younger adults,” he said.
He added that around 20-25% of lung cancer cases occur in never-smokers, who are mostly women. “I have no doubt air pollution from secondhand smoke and the haze are major risk factors.”
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Malaysia. It is also the second most-common cancer among Malaysian men and among the most deadly cancers affecting women.
In the shorter term, haze can trigger or worsen asthma and bronchitis in susceptible people, while irritating the airways and increasing phlegm and other respiratory symptoms.
Avoiding exposure not equally possible for everyone
At Nasi Lemak Pak Man in Shah Alam, co-owner Farrrah Adeeba said the eatery’s open-concept setup means haze can easily enter the premises.

“Our staff are exposed much longer than customers, sometimes the whole working day," she told FMT Lifestyle. “If the haze gets worse, staff health becomes our main concern. We may need masks, shorter shifts or adjustments depending on the air quality.”

For now, the haze has not significantly affected the restaurant’s business. Farrrah said Malaysians have become accustomed to such conditions and tend to carry on with their routines unless the situation becomes particularly severe.

If the haze persists or reaches unhealthy levels, however, she expects the impact to extend beyond health. “People will stay indoors more, families may avoid going out, and that will eventually affect sales."

The uncertainty also extends to what businesses should do if conditions deteriorate further. Farrrah, who runs several other F&B businesses, hopes the authorities can provide clear guidelines early, including what action businesses should take at different air-quality levels.
She also wants greater protection for workers who cannot simply remain indoors.
“Most importantly, address the haze problem at the source, not only when it becomes an emergency,” she stressed.
Anand said practical measures such as limiting outdoor activities, reducing work shifts where possible, wearing masks, staying hydrated and using air purifiers may help reduce exposure.

- 'Fine margins' -

Carrick has three weeks to stew on United's miserable start during an extended international break.
Questions about United's transfer policy and fitness regime are growing louder.
The 45-year-old must come up with answers before they return to action with a crucial clash against bottom-of-the-table Tottenham on October 10.
Losing to Roberto De Zerbi's side would be a huge blow to Carrick's hopes of turning the tide, especially with tricky trips to Atletico Madrid and Leeds looming after Tottenham visit Old Trafford.
But Carrick is putting his faith in United's players absorbing the lessons from their painful start.
"You learn about each other, they learn about me, I learn about the individual and as a team, how we respond, what our reaction is," he said.
"That's part of growing as a group. You have to go through certain things to get to the end of it."

372a0714d1439f8f: SAINT PIERRE: French President Emmanuel Macron and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney announced closer ties Sunday, speaking from France's tiny territory of Saint Pierre and Miquelon, just off Canada's Atlantic coast.
Their meeting came at a time when both countries are experiencing strained relations with the US.
"We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so," said Macron at their joint news conference.
"History remembers those who... defend their sovereignty, those who stay true to their values," said Carney in his speech.
Earlier, both leaders had paid their respects at a monument honouring those islanders who volunteered for the Free French forces during WWII.
Carney said the moment had come to tighten bonds with France and the European Union, following up on a successful visit to Brussels, when the EU offered Canada "associate member" status.
Macron said the two countries would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy.
Carney proposed that France, Canada, the US and China work together on artificial intelligence.
Earlier Sunday, Macron was waiting for Carney, the first Canadian prime minister to visit the territory, when he stepped off the plane.
The two leaders greeted each other with a warm handshake and a long embrace in the bright sunshine.
"In a world in crisis, our friendship is a strength," Macron posted on X, above a video of him welcoming Carney.
"Together, we affirm our sovereignty, our freedom to decide and our willingness to build a future of peace and prosperity."
Carney also posted a video of their greeting on his X account. "Good to see you, my friend," he said, posting in English and in French.
Tensions with US
The trip carries significant symbolic resonance.
The archipelago is France's only remaining possession in North America, a vestige of the vast territories Paris once controlled in what is now Canada and the United States.
Macron argues that US President Donald Trump's second mandate has reinforced the case he has promoted that Europe needs to become more sovereign, especially on security.
Carney, caught up in an intensifying dispute with Trump -- who has even threatened to annex Canada -- has welcomed a proposal for his country to become the European Union's first "associate member".
He has described his nation as "the most European of non-European countries".
Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state have been strongly rejected by Ottawa.

Last Monday, Trump posted an image to social media with a map of North America in which Canada, Greenland and Mexico, much of central America and the Caribbean, as well as Iceland, were coloured in with the US flag.
The image also encompassed several French overseas territories, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique -- and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.
But the territory is French, Macron reaffirmed on his arrival in the territory late Saturday, dismissing "strange ideas" on the subject.
'Common values'

The joint visit was to underscore that Canada and France share "the same values of freedom, democracy, the rule of law and respect for the sovereignty of nations", the French president's office said ahead of the meeting.
That was certainly the message at Sunday's joint news conference. And if neither mentioned Trump by name, his influence seemed to inform both leaders' speeches.
"We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for free and fair trade, the science on which our decisions are based, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," said Macron.
"And this is what very deeply unites Canada and France, Canada and the European Union," he added.
Carney said: "The time has come to tighten our links between Canada and France, between Canada and the European Union -- links based on the values we share."
The archipelago is one of several strategically located French overseas territories that span the globe.
Macron's three-day visit to the French territory, an archipelago of fewer than 6,000 people a short distance from Newfoundland, is the first by a French president in more than a decade.

304c1c3868916a52: PUTRAJAYA, Sept 20 — The return of the haze across parts of Malaysia has once again brought forest and land fires in the region into focus.
But as smoke spreads and satellite images light up with hotspots, the question of where the fires are and what caused them is not as straightforward as it may appear.
Malaysia’s response this time includes an offer of firefighting assistance to Indonesia, which reflects the fact that the haze does not stop at national borders.

Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on Thursday said Malaysia had offered a Bombardier CL-415MP aircraft, three helicopters and 52 officers and personnel from the National Disaster Management Agency, Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) and the Royal Malaysian Air Force.
The offer was conveyed to Indonesian vice-president Gibran Rakabuming Raka during his four-day working visit to Indonesia. It will be referred to President Prabowo Subianto for approval.
The CL-415MP, operated by MMEA, is capable of aerial firefighting. It was previously deployed to South Sumatra in 2015, when it dropped 546,000 litres of water during a five-day operation.
Ahmad Zahid, who is also the National Disaster Management Committee chairman, said the offer to assist was to help Indonesia tackle transboundary haze, rather than interfering in its affairs.
The urgency is clear from the air quality readings in Malaysia.
As at 5pm on Friday, 32 areas recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings.

According to the Malaysian Air Pollutant Index Management System portal, Johan Setia in Selangor recorded the highest reading at 183, followed by Shah Alam (169), Petaling Jaya (162), Banting (161) and Klang (159).

Sarawak recorded the highest number of affected areas, with Kuching recording an API reading of 174, followed by Samarahan (167), IPD Serian (166), Sibu (162), Bintulu (161), Sarikei (155), Sri Aman (154) and Kapit (153).
Putrajaya recorded an unhealthy reading of 172, while Batu Muda and Cheras recorded 167 and 165, respectively. Temerloh and Jerantut in Pahang recorded 155 and 151.
An API reading of 0 to 50 indicates good air quality; 51 to 100, moderate; 101 to 200, unhealthy; 201 to 300, very unhealthy; and 301 and above, hazardous.
For the public, the immediate concern is the smoke. For those trying to trace the fires, however, the picture is more complicated.
Indonesia was reported as saying that it was complying with Asean’s existing haze response mechanisms, including daily reporting of hotspot data, projected smoke movements and firefighting measures.
Asean activated a Level 3 alert for severe transboundary haze on August 26. Under the mechanism, member states share information to help neighbouring countries take precautionary measures.
At the same time, the haze has once again revived questions about the role of the palm oil industry in regional fires.

The Malaysian Palm Oil Board (MPOB), however, said regional forest and peat fires could not be attributed primarily to oil-palm cultivation, with satellite mapping currently showing hotspots across multiple land uses.
These, it said, include unmanaged areas, pulpwood plantations and small-scale farming plots.
Director-General (DG) Datuk Badrul Hisham Mohd said human land-clearing activities remained a major driver of fires, while severe climate anomalies such as El Niño could amplify their spread.
“From a scientific standpoint, El Niño and prolonged dry weather act strictly as environmental amplifiers, not the spark itself,” he told Bernama.
That distinction matters when looking at the fires.
Badrul Hisham said wildfires did not occur spontaneously in the region’s humid climate, with ignition generally associated with human activity.
Prolonged dry weather, however, reduces soil and vegetation moisture, allowing fires to spread more rapidly.
The problem becomes harder to manage in peat areas, where drained peat can dry out and burn below the surface.
Badrul Hisham said this can make fires difficult to detect and extinguish.
“Once ignited, peat fires can continue smouldering underground and may reignite even after surface fires appear to have been brought under control.
“The resulting emissions can continue for weeks or months and, depending on wind direction, contribute to prolonged transboundary haze,” he said.
When fire risk rises

The newly-appointed DG also stressed that the Malaysian oil palm industry should not be described as having a seasonal open-burning practice because zero burning has already been established within the industry through the mandatory Malaysian Sustainable Palm Oil (MSPO) Certification Scheme, enforced since January 2020.
It is the risk of fire that changes with the seasons, he said.

That risk generally increases during prolonged dry periods, particularly from June to September during the southwest monsoon, while some regions also experience a dry window around January and February.

Lower rainfall, declining soil and peat moisture and higher temperatures during these periods make accidental or unauthorised ignition more likely to spread, with El Niño capable of further intensifying the risk.
There is also a need to be careful when reading satellite hotspot maps.
A hotspot is an indicator of possible fire. It is not, by itself, proof of open burning or evidence of someone starting a fire.
“That distinction matters, because a hotspot can identify where a fire may be occurring, but not necessarily who started it, or what land use is involved.
“For Malaysia and Indonesia, therefore, the immediate challenge is twofold: containing the fires and improving the ability to identify their causes,” he said.
For now, Malaysia’s offer of aircraft, helicopters and personnel is focused on putting out fires.
But the wider haze problem is unlikely to be solved by firefighting alone.
Prevention, land management and early detection remain part of the equation, as does cooperation between countries sharing the same airspace and, at times, the same smoke.
The palm oil debate will continue, particularly whenever the haze returns.
Therefore, satellite hotspots alone cannot settle that debate. Fires occur across different types of land, and weather conditions can determine how quickly they spread and how long they persist.
That makes identifying the actual source and cause of each fire just as important as putting it out.
For Malaysia, Indonesia and the wider region, that may be the more difficult part of dealing with the haze. — Bernama
4a6b04ffefce7040: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 20 — Jazeman Firhan Jaafar, 33, has spent more than two decades in motorsport, from racing internationally and coming within reach of a Formula One seat to competing at Le Mans.
Today, the former Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula One development driver is using that experience to open doors for Malaysian talent in motorsport and the wider automotive industry.

Through Persona Energy Sdn Bhd, the company he established in 2018, Jazeman runs the Technology Transfer Apprenticeship Programme (TTAP), giving Malaysian engineers, mechanics and other technical talents hands-on exposure to international motorsport and industry partners. “So, I have talents like that … they have the grit, the skill, but they don’t have that ‘door opening’. So, I open the door for them,” Jazeman told Bernama in an interview recently.

So far, 95 talents have gone through TTAP, with most already working in the industry while some have pursued further studies. Supported by partners including Porsche, Bosch Engineering and Yayasan Raja Muda Selangor, the programme exposes participants to areas ranging from race cars and data to vehicle components and engineering.

TTAP runs for seven months, with participants required to gain hands-on experience at three races during the programme. The locations vary according to the racing calendar, with participants potentially assigned to events in Malaysia, Japan, Thailand or Indonesia.

Jazeman said some are subsequently taken to additional races once the teams are comfortable with their performance. “So, my requirement is three races. I do a pre-event briefing. Then, we do a scorecard to see their performance and then their graduation,” he elaborated.
He wants TTAP to eventually become self-sustaining, with between 10 and 20 Malaysian talents integrated into the racing industry each year, before expanding the programme to talents across Asean.
From six-year-old go-karter to Europe

Jazeman’s own journey began almost by chance. He was six in 1998 when a friend of his late father invited him to try go-karting in Shah Alam. What began with rented or leased karts progressed to national and Asian championships. By eight, Jazeman had decided he wanted to become a Formula One (F1) driver. His mother, however, insisted that racing could not come at the expense of his education. “I had to promise her to never forget to ‘mengaji’ (study) first. You know, do my tuition first. And then I can go racing,” he recalled.

At 14, Jazeman was below the minimum age requirement for the Petronas Talent Development Programme’s Formula BMW programme. He instead secured an exemption from the FIA to compete in Formula BMW Asia and found his own sponsorship. He won the championship, beating the Petronas team. A day later, Petronas called and invited him to join its programme.

At 15, Jazeman moved to Europe, where he spent much of the next nine years pursuing a professional racing career. “I didn’t have a life like other teenagers did. I had to move, and I didn’t have many friends in Europe either. I probably had one friend who happened to study there. But then I built my contacts; I built my relationships with certain people from racing, and that led me to my professional career then. So, I was in the UK nine years in total. No easy feat lah,” he recalled.
Europe exposed him to a mature motorsport industry and eventually took him to the final step before F1.
The F1 deal that did not happen

After winning the Formula Renault 3.5 Series race in Monaco in 2015, Jazeman said he received offers from two F1 teams, Force India and Manor. Force India presented what he described as the stronger proposition: a one-plus-one-year deal, beginning as a reserve driver before progressing to a race seat. The challenge was securing the necessary financial backing within a limited timeframe.

Jazeman said a proposed funding structure involved Petronas, tourism and sports authorities as well as corporate sponsors. But the plan came amid political pressure surrounding the 1Malaysia Development Bhd controversy, while falling oil prices put pressure on Petronas.

He tried to salvage the offer, but the required commitments could not be confirmed in time. “They came back with a second offer to proceed with reserve driver (first). I still have the contracts in my mum’s house. But we couldn’t sign it because none of the sponsors could confirm at that time,” he recalled.

He subsequently redirected his career towards Mercedes-AMG and endurance racing, which offered the prospect of a longer professional career. “I’m honoured and blessed that I was given an opportunity. You know, I was on that final step. But I think we tried our best,” he added.

Jazeman acknowledged that they could perhaps have negotiated better, but said F1 deals required people who understood how to put the different elements together. Today, that chapter is closed. “So if you ask me again if I would try again, no. I think I’ve moved on from it,” he said.
Unfinished business

Jazeman has not, however, moved on entirely from racing. He has gone on to compete in GT and endurance racing and still believes he can perform at a high level. One race in particular remains unfinished business: the 24 Hours of Le Mans, the world’s premier sports car endurance race, won by the team covering the furthest distance in 24 hours.

Jazeman competed at Le Mans in 2018 in an all-Malaysian line-up with Weiron Tan and Nabil Jeffri, finishing fourth in the LMP2 class. “I have been honoured to have won big races. The list goes on,” he recollected. “If you put me in a race car tomorrow, I will perform at my utmost best. But Formula 1, no.”
Jazeman’s experience has also shaped how he views Malaysia’s search for another F1 driver.
He believes Malaysia has talent with the potential to build professional racing careers, although the pathway to F1 has become considerably more demanding as the sport has evolved.

Malaysia has talent capable of professional careers in GT, Le Mans and endurance racing, Jazeman reckons, but reaching F3, F2 and ultimately F1 requires more than funding, as it also demands enormous early sacrifices, including leaving home and building a career overseas as he did at 15.
The talent Malaysia left on the table
Having spent years racing overseas, Jazeman believes Malaysia has historically paid too little attention to developing the people behind the race car.

The country once had extensive links with F1 through Malaysian companies and organisations, yet much of that involvement remained commercial rather than being systematically used to develop local technical talent.

“Because a lot of the involvement in F1 was purely a commercial element. Not to grasp at talent development. Which is such a pity,” he said, adding that at its peak, Malaysian interests were connected with as many as four F1 teams. We had four F1 teams from a small country. But no F1 driver, no F1 engineer. So, I don’t know what the sole purpose of this commercial element was. Talent development or talent in the team should be the core. That is how I see it,” said Jazeman.

He is also convinced Malaysia has technical talent capable of working at the highest levels of motorsport. “You know, race teams, international race teams love hiring Malaysians because we speak English. I’m certain our talents can do it,” he added.
Beyond hosting
The question of what Malaysia gains from international motorsport is again relevant as Sepang prepares to host the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia next month.

Jazeman noted that Malaysia already has the facilities and hospitality needed to host major motorsport events. Where Malaysia falls short, he believes, is in extracting more lasting benefits from the international teams and organisations that come here. “We have the opportunity to ask them for what we want. I feel that we do not capitalise enough on the spillover effects,” he added.

While Malaysia already benefits from business spillovers such as hotels and transport, Jazeman said more could be done in talent development and technology transfer. He pointed to the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) choosing Malaysia to host the International Karting World Cup twice as evidence that the country’s facilities and grassroots ecosystem have international recognition.

“Now, what falls short is that maybe we are a bit shy to squeeze from them what we want because we may not be paying for F1 today, but we still have the top teams coming here. We have the opportunity to ask (for) what we want. I feel that we do not capitalise enough on the spillover effects,” he reiterated.

Jazeman reckons Malaysia has at times placed greater emphasis on hosting major races than building the ecosystem beneath them. He said there was coordination among the Sepang International Circuit, the Motorsports Association of Malaysia and the Youth and Sports Ministry, but the government ultimately had to lead on what Malaysia wanted to develop.

“We had F1 that came here for many years, but we didn’t capitalise. So now, we have an interest to come back, and people want it to be back permanently, but we have to really plan for that integration … but it has to come from the ministry. You want to champion the best engineers of F1 of tomorrow; it has to come from them. You want the next F1 driver; it has to come from them,” he said.
For Jazeman, TTAP is one attempt to change that. He wants the programme to become sustainable, build more links with international teams and eventually extend its pathway beyond Malaysia.

After spending his youth trying to find a way into the highest levels of motorsport, he is now opening that door for others. “The door is open; you go for it. That is the only thing I can do, which I have done,” said Jazeman. — Bernama
d17c941c3f34adf1: CAPAS (Philippines), Sept 20 — Tribal leader Petronila Munoz walked across the sweeping Philippine grasslands she has called home for generations, uncertain about its future, as a sprawling tech hub for a US-led initiative takes shape.

With little information and no prior consultation, the Indigenous chieftain said her Aeta Hungey tribe was uncertain how much of their land could be affected or what will become of the livelihood it provides.
“There’s still no clarity,” Munoz told AFP inside the tribe’s traditional meeting hall.
“What will happen to us? That’s our biggest question.”

In April, the United States announced that the Philippines had joined Pax Silica, a US-led effort to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors and rare earth elements and reduce participating countries’ dependence on China.

The Philippines has designated a 1,620-hectare (4,000-acre) site in New Clark City in Tarlac province, north of Manila, for a manufacturing hub aimed at producing high-end components for use in artificial intelligence data centres.
The government estimates the initiative could attract up to US$70 billion in investment and create about 190,000 jobs, a major boost to a country with more than three million unemployed people.
The project has a long timeline. No tenants have been confirmed.
Plans to domestically process the country’s mineral resources could be even further away.
For about 1,000 Aetas, however, the prospect of displacement is already here.
In July, they received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) warning that the project “could affect your occupied lands”.
‘Money runs out’

Munoz said visiting BCDA employees told them to leave by December and relocate to an area about 16 kilometres (10 miles) from their current home, without providing a master plan showing which parts of their ancestral domains would be affected.
Munoz said the BCDA has offered them just 30 pesos (US$0.48) per square metre for their lands, an offer all declined.
“Our lives, our livelihood and our culture are tied to this ancestral land,” Munoz said.
“Land is more important. Money runs out.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Residents looking at a map with proposed projects by the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) in Capas. — AFP pic
The BCDA declined to address specific questions about the Aetas’ situation and rejected a freedom of information request for the site’s official boundary map and geospatial data.
It said the information was being “withheld temporarily until the official action is finalized or published”.
At a Senate hearing last month, BCDA president Joshua Bingcang said the Aetas were living on government land. Like many Indigenous groups in the Philippines, they hold no land title.
Civic groups have also raised concerns about the project’s environmental impact, particularly the demand for water and electricity in a country plagued by droughts and rotational power outages.
The US Statement Department told AFP that “environmental, water, energy, and community-impact studies” would inform the project’s design.
“Before any major development happens, we expect rigorous stakeholder impact assessments will take place,” a spokesperson said.
Bingcang told the Senate that investors would be required to build their own power and water systems.
‘We have to open up’

Alvin Camba, research director at an AI firm focused on supply chains and risk assessment, said Manila’s close relationship with the United States could motivate investors to set up shop despite the power concerns.
Last month, reports said Washington planned to warn countries they could be excluded from Pax Silica if they joined a rival framework backed by Beijing.

“This is where the advantage of the Philippines comes in. The Philippines is the least affected by Chinese capital in South-east Asia,” Camba told AFP, saying the country would offer foreign companies the ability to “disentangle” from China.
For political economist Calixto Chikiamco, Pax Silica represents a “historic opportunity” for the Philippines to move beyond its traditional wheelhouse of microchip testing and packaging.
“We have to open up to foreign investment so that technology transfer (to the Philippines) will happen,” he told AFP.
Sacrifices
The BCDA has been conducting public consultations in Tarlac and nearby provinces, but the agency has yet to hold talks with her tribe, Munoz said.
The Aetas remain uncertain if the government would help them build new homes or provide land to cultivate for income if they are moved.
“I wish they would listen to us. They’re just talking among themselves,” she said, adding she worried her tribe would not be qualified for the sort of new jobs Pax Silica promised.
While a proponent of the initiative, Chikiamco said the government was doing “a terrible job” explaining the benefits and tradeoffs it represented.
Camba agreed: “I would actually advise the Philippine government to be very transparent about what’s happening. A big problem is transparency.”
Still, the benefits outweigh the risks, he said.
“Every country that has... jump-started development has had to make sacrifices,” Camba said.
But 63-year-old Munoz, who hopes to be buried in her tribe’s traditional burial ground, said she would not leave, even if a backhoe flattened her home.
“Why do we have to be the ones to sacrifice for the kind of development they want?” she asked. — AFP

fc1c80d2f52de6a5: SEPTEMBER 20 — When agarwood (gaharu) is mentioned, many of us might immediately think of aromatic wood burned for its distinctive fragrance or processed into expensive perfumes and oils. Yet behind its unmistakable scent, lies economic potential that extends far beyond these traditional uses - a potential that remains largely untapped.

Agarwood is more than a valuable forest resource. With the right combination of research, technology, innovation and marketing, this natural treasure can be transformed into a diverse range of value-added products, opening new opportunities for local entrepreneurs and industries.

The karas tree, particularly Aquilaria malaccensis, is among the species associated with the production of agarwood. Its uniqueness lies in the formation of resin-rich wood that produces its distinctive aroma. This remarkable characteristic has given agarwood a long history of use, particularly in fragrances, cultural practices and traditional medicine.
Beyond fragrance

The perception that agarwood is valuable only as aromatic wood or perfume oil needs to be changed. In today’s vibrant economy, the value of a natural resource is no longer determined solely by the price of its raw material. More importantly, value lies in how effectively that resource can be converted into marketable, value-added products.
This is where innovation becomes essential.

Rather than simply selling natural resources in their raw form, local industries need to move proactively into downstream product development, research and development (R&D), branding and marketing. The greater our ability to create value from local resources, the greater their potential contribution to industry and the national economy.

Technological advances are also opening new possibilities for the agarwood industry. Scientific methods can now be used to evaluate the quality of agarwood and its oil, including analyses of their composition and chemical characteristics. Such developments demonstrate that agarwood should no longer be viewed solely as part of a traditional industry. It has considerable potential to develop into a knowledge-driven industry supported by research, science and technology.

This view is shared by Aminudin Md Hafidzin, an entrepreneur and researcher actively involved in agarwood-related research. The participation of industry players in research is particularly important because the future of the sector will depend on their ability to move beyond supplying raw materials towards creating commercially valuable innovations.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

The author argues that Malaysia should move agarwood beyond raw-resource exports by building a research-driven, value-added industry around innovation, branding, market insight and local products. — AFP pic
Unlocking opportunities for local industry

Undeniably, Malaysia has an advantage. Agarwood is not an unfamiliar resource in this country. Yet the availability of a valuable natural resource alone does not guarantee the success of an industry. The real question, therefore, is how Malaysia can unlock the full potential of agarwood by transforming this natural treasure into innovative, high-value products that command strong brand recognition and sustainable market demand.
This is the challenge facing local industry.

Among the local industry players exploring the commercial potential of agarwood-based products is Malga Industries Sdn Bhd, a Bumiputera company with extensive experience in agarwood-related research. One of the company’s latest innovations is Malga Gold Plus, a product formulated from premium-grade distilled agarwood water extracted from agarwood trees and developed for its potential health-related applications.

What is particularly significant is not simply the creation of a new product, but how research and innovation can transform agarwood from a valuable natural resource into high-value downstream products with strong commercial potential. It demonstrates that the value of agarwood need not end with the sale of raw wood or the distillation of oil. Through innovation, agarwood can be brought closer to consumers through the development of new products and applications. According to Bukhari Rusli, Marketing Manager of Malga Gold Plus, the company’s various research and market development initiatives indicate that downstream agarwood products have room to grow beyond the resource’s conventional uses.

Such developments matter to Malaysia’s local industries. The country should not allow the value of its natural resources to end at the raw-material stage while greater economic returns from processing, innovation, branding and marketing are captured elsewhere.
From natural resource to marketable brand
The next challenge is the market.

Creating an innovative product is only part of the journey. A product must also earn consumer confidence and market acceptance. Today’s consumers have unprecedented access to information. Before making a purchase, they compare products and prices, read the experiences of other consumers and seek information through various platforms. Therefore, companies developing agarwood-based products must therefore understand more than the technical characteristics of their products. They must also understand the people who buy and use them. These are important questions for the future of the industry.

This is where market research becomes an important bridge between agarwood innovation and the consumer. The potential of agarwood does not depend solely on the uniqueness of the resource or the novelty of the products developed from it. It also depends on whether those products meet consumer needs and gain market acceptance.

Decisions about developing and marketing agarwood-based products should therefore not be based on assumptions alone. Consumer data and feedback can help businesses better understand market acceptance, satisfaction and trust, while identifying more effective marketing strategies.

Collaboration between the agarwood industry and academic researchers can also become an important catalyst for the sector’s development. Researchers in marketing and consumer behaviour, for example, can help businesses better understand their markets, while expertise in science and technology can support further research and product development. When academic research expertise is combined with the practical knowledge and experience of industry players, agarwood can become more than an object of study. It can provide the foundation for commercially viable innovations that respond to genuine consumer needs.

It is this synergy between research, industry and the market that can help ensure Malaysian agarwood is recognised not merely as a valuable natural resource, but also as the foundation for competitive local products and brands.
Building a Malaysian agarwood brand
It is time to view agarwood from a much broader perspective.

The question should no longer be simply how much a kilogramme of agarwood is worth or how expensive its oil can be. The bigger question is how Malaysia can develop the entire agarwood value chain; from cultivation and resource production to research, processing, product development, branding and marketing. We have the natural resources. We have researchers. We also have entrepreneurs and local companies willing to explore new opportunities. What is needed is an ecosystem capable of bringing these strengths together.

If Malaysia can combine its natural resources with research, technology, entrepreneurial creativity and a deeper understanding of consumers, agarwood has the potential to become part of the country’s high-value product industry.

The efforts of local companies such as Malga Industries Sdn Bhd to explore the development of agarwood-based products demonstrate that opportunities for innovation do exist. To take the industry further, however, stronger collaboration among growers, businesses, universities, researchers and relevant agencies will be essential.

Malaysia should aspire to be more than simply a country blessed with agarwood resources. The greater ambition should be to build Malaysian knowledge, innovation, products and agarwood brands capable of creating value for the national economy and competing in wider markets. Agarwood has long been treasured for its fragrance. The challenge now is to ensure that its fragrance carries with it the name of Malaysian innovation to the world.
* Professor Dr Nor Azila Mohd Noor is attached to the School of Business Management, Universiti Utara Malaysia.
** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
a1e749a7f8ab8d68: Before two of its alleged members were arrested and charged in Australia last month, the hacker group known as TeamPCP carried out a hacking spree unlike any other in history. It tainted hundreds of open-source programs with its malware, stole developer accounts to perpetuate that software supply-chain hacking, and even released a Dune-themed self-spreading worm to automate the process, ultimately breaching more than a thousand companies.

Now Google’s threat intelligence group has revealed that during a key moment of TeamPCP’s rampage, the company’s own undercover researcher had infiltrated the group—allowing Google to monitor the hacking spree from the inside, warn breach targets, and even help disrupt the group’s attempts to exploit those victims.

In a talk at security firm SentinelOne's LABScon research conference today, Google Threat Intelligence Group researcher Austin Larsen will present details on the company’s investigation—and infiltration—of TeamPCP amidst the group’s unprecedented, chaotic supply-chain hacking campaign. According to Larsen, Google eventually followed a trail of operational security mistakes allegedly made by one of the two Australians now accused of being leading members of the hacker group and passed on key identifying details to law enforcement. The company also received intelligence from ShinyHunters, another infamous cybercriminal group that TeamPCP partnered with, but which later turned on the supply-chain hackers. And perhaps most surprisingly, Larsen says that Google’s security subsidiary Mandiant had an undercover analyst—not himself—within the group’s inner circle from almost the beginning of TeamPCP’s time in the spotlight.
7e6c02c479d86de7: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 20 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said he will meet Transport Minister Anthony Loke to hear his views before deciding whether to accept his resignation.

Anwar said Loke had informed him of his intention to step down following the conditional pardon granted to former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak but had yet to submit a formal resignation letter.
Speaking to media in Shah Alam today, Anwar said he wanted to sit down with Loke before making any decision.
“I have to listen to his views, and I understand because he is a principled person.

“From the very beginning, he has been consistent in opposing measures that could give the impression that we are weak or lenient towards corrupt practices — especially when action is taken against many others, including those involved in petty corruption.
“Therefore, it is best that I meet him and hear his perspective,” Anwar said.

Anwar said Loke had informed him of the decision after chairing an emergency DAP central executive committee (CEC) meeting yesterday, but told him he would bring the resignation letter when they met to discuss the matter.
“He [Loke] held a meeting yesterday and informed me about it. He said he would bring the letter when we meet to discuss the matter.
“I told him, ‘It’s fine, whenever we have the time.’
“After this, I will be heading to Melaka. Tomorrow, he will be leaving for Shanghai, while I will be going to Shanghai on Tuesday for a meeting with Premier Li Qiang,” he said.
Asked about the possibility of a Cabinet dissolution, Anwar said the government was taking matters “one by one” for now.

Loke, who is also DAP secretary-general, announced yesterday that he had offered to resign as transport minister following a nearly three-hour emergency CEC meeting at the party’s headquarters in Pudu.
He said he would submit his resignation letter to Anwar soon, while remaining DAP secretary-general and Seremban MP. Other DAP ministers and deputy ministers will remain in the government.

971963f355d3d7af: PARIS, Sept 20 — Paris Saint-Germain’s Qatari President Nasser al-Khelaifi is under investigation in France on conflict-of-interest suspicions, prosecutors in the French capital said on Sunday.

The preliminary probe is linked to his twin stewardship of the Champions League title holders and the beIN Media Group and involves a meeting on broadcasting rights with the football league’s representatives in July 2024, the prosecutor’s office said, confirming a report in L’Equipe sports newspaper.

52e2c4e785e58838: TOKYO, Sept 20 — China’s 13-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi warned she could go even faster after smashing an Asian Games record to win gold in Japan on Sunday, two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics.

Yu, who turns 14 next month, romped home in the women’s 200m butterfly in 2min 05.08sec to shave almost half a second off the time set by compatriot Zhang Yufei three years ago in Hangzhou of 2:05:57.
The teenager’s time in winning her first major gold medal was 3.36sec faster than team-mate Chang Mohan in silver.
It was the first of three individual events Yu is scheduled to compete in at the Asian Games, where swimming is being held in Tokyo.
“It was only so-so,” a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal.
“I hope I can swim even faster. I improved my time by 0.9 seconds here, and I believe I will perform better next time.”
Yu became the youngest swimming world championships medallist in history last year when she won bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China’s 4x200m freestyle relay team.
She also finished a whisker outside the medals in fourth in three world individual events.
She has embellished her growing reputation this year, notably with a victory over multiple American Olympic champion Regan Smith in March.
But she said her “technique is still slightly lacking” after crushing the field in her Asian Games debut.
“I need to lower my head earlier, reach farther forward and improve the movement of my legs,” she said.
“Those are all areas that I need to work on.”
The schoolgirl with the pixie haircut is expected to be a serious contender at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
But she has spoken of struggling to deal with the heavy load placed on her.
During the build-up to last year’s China National Games she said the pressure of wanting to win the 400m medley nearly became too much.
Her coach told her to persevere and “believe in yourself”, she said.
Yu went on to win four medals at the National Games.
Some in the swimming world have questioned the mental and physical impact of high-level training and competing on Yu at such a young age. — AFP

277de5d0973d0aa9: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 20 — The childcare profession should be regarded as an important component in supporting the family economy and not merely as a job involving the care of children, said the Prime Minister’s Senior Political Adviser Tengku Datuk Seri Zafrul Tengku Abdul Aziz.

He said having trusted childcare providers enabled parents to work with greater peace of mind while ensuring that their children received proper care, making the childcare sector part of the country’s economic and social support ecosystem.
“We need to change the perception that it is merely a job. The reality is that the childcare profession is closely linked to parents’ ability to work.

“Looking after those who care for our children is the same as looking after Malaysia’s future,” he said in his speech at the opening of the Central Zone Gala Pesona Kasih Madani at the Ampang Jaya Municipal Council Convention Centre, Taman Melawati, here today.

Tengku Zafrul said his experience interacting with communities had also shown how families relied heavily on trusted childcare providers, particularly to enable parents to continue working while ensuring their children’s welfare was taken care of.

He also said that training, certification, recognition and legislation relating to childcare should continue to be prioritised to ensure that the profession had stronger standards and received due recognition.

In this regard, he said the views and challenges shared by childcare providers through the programme would be brought to the Finance Ministry and the prime minister for consideration in the Budget 2027 planning, including aspects of support, training, certification and the expansion of related programmes.

About 600 informal childcare providers, family members, mentors, programme partners and stakeholders attended the Central Zone Gala Pesona Kasih Madani, which was organised to strengthen the knowledge, skills and level of professionalism of home-based childcare providers in Malaysia.

Since its launch in August 2025, Kasih Madani has reached more than 1,000 childcare providers in four states — Kuala Lumpur, Perak, Kedah and Penang — through programmes such as the Madani Childcare Pilot Course (KARISMA), Madani Childcare Seminar (SEMAI) and Madani Childcare Professionalisation Skills Mentoring (BITARA).

The initiative, implemented by Merdeka Center with the support of Yayasan Sime Darby and the Ministry of Finance through Budget 2026, also focuses on skills development, career planning, leadership, personal branding and mentoring to strengthen the professionalism of childcare providers. — Bernama
e751e956ffdc3f3e: NAGOYA, Sept 20 — Myanmar’s Wai Khin Hnin on Sunday became the first Asian Games gold medallist in teqball, an acrobatic football-table tennis hybrid making its debut at this year’s event in Japan.
Watched by Barcelona and Spain football legend Carles Puyol, Wai Khin Hnin beat Indonesia’s Sumaya, who goes by one name, 2-1 in the final to capture the inaugural women’s singles title.

Wai Khin Hnin lost the first set of the final but came back to win 10-12, 12-8, 12-9 and claim gold.
“I’m delighted, I’m thankful to my head coach for believing in me and selecting me to play in the women’s singles. I believed that I could do it,” she said.
“My next goal is to win the gold medal for Myanmar at the 2027 SEA Games.”
The competition has seen a diverse range of players vying to become the Asian Games’ first teqball medallists.
The Philippines men’s team featured three 14-year-olds including Prince Agustin, who lost in the singles bronze-medal match.
Japan were represented by Takahiro Nodomi, who also works as a comedian.
“I played football until high school, gave up, started teqball in my late 30s, and made it to this big stage at 40,” he said.
“If the message that ‘even old guys can work hard’ reached everyone, then I feel I was able to release some ‘old guy power’.”

Kuwait’s Basel Ahmad and Abdulwahab Alqattan (in blue) play a point against Indonesia’s Husni Uba and La Ode Mardan during their men’s doubles bronze medal teqball match at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya on September 20, 2026. — AFP pic

4a5395359fcb3662: KOTA BHARU, Sept 20 — A 75-year-old retired teacher in Bachok lost about RM15,000 after being duped by a scam syndicate posing as police officers, which also resulted in the victim handing over two ATM cards and his wife’s gold necklace with a pendant.
Kelantan Police Chief Datuk Mohd Yusoff Mamat said that the police arrested a 31-year-old woman on September 13 around Kota Bharu to assist with the investigation of the case.
He said the incident began on September 12 when the victim received a phone call from an individual claiming to be a police officer from the Johor Contingent Police Headquarters (IPK).
“The victim was informed that he had a court summons amounting to RM25,000 and was accused of being involved in money laundering and a drug syndicate, which carries a 15-year prison sentence.
“The call was then transferred to another individual claiming to be a senior Bukit Aman police officer via WhatsApp,” he said in a statement today.

Mohd Yusoff said the victim was then instructed to keep the matter secret from anyone before being asked to surrender two ATM cards and his wife’s gold necklace with a pendant, purportedly to be handed over to an investigating officer who would come to his house.
He mentioned that at about 5:00 pm on the same day, a woman arrived in a car at the victim’s house, collected the items, and left.
“The gold necklace was subsequently sold at a gold shop in Kota Bharu on the same day, while a portion of the proceeds from the sale was deposited into a third-party account.
“Based on preliminary statements, the suspect received instructions via WhatsApp from an unidentified individual to collect the victim’s items,” he said.
However, he noted that the victim managed to contact the bank to block the ATM cards, and no transactions were detected.

According to him, the police seized the victim’s two ATM cards, a Perodua Axia car, a bank-in receipt, and a gold shop receipt, while the gold necklace was successfully recovered from the respective gold shop.
“The case is being investigated under Section 420 of the Penal Code,” he said.

Mohd Yusoff advised the public not to panic or be deceived by threats of summonses and arrests, reminding them that the police, courts, Bank Negara Malaysia, and banking institutions will never contact members of the public to ask them to surrender ATM cards, PIN numbers, or jewellery to any party. — Bernama
3f22b785bad84e36: Ferrari’s two-seat sports cars might be the brand’s identity, but the Italian automaker has always catered to customers who want to bring more than one passenger along for the ride. It started building cars with back seats in the 1960s with the 250 GT 2+2; as the name suggests, the second row was more for occasional use, something that was true all the way through to the 612 in the early 2000s. Ferrari followed with its first true four-seater, the all-wheel drive FF, which adopted "Breadvan" styling. Its first hatchback was still a three-door, though, and slightly more practical for carrying cargo rather than humans in the rear. That was true for the GTC4 that followed, too. But with the Purosangue, the rear passengers have been given something of an upgrade.

For one thing, there is an extra pair of doors, rear-hinged ones that provide direct access to the pair of rear bucket seats. There’s still a rear hatch, so this is technically a five-door. But there’s an immovable firewall between the cargo area and the passenger cabin, and the rear seats do not fold flat. So unlike the 21st century breadvans we have previously reviewed, a Costco run in the Purosangue might be possible, but you’re probably going to want a roof rack if you plan to go skiing, cycling, or anything else that requires bulky equipment. It’s also probably accurate that Ferrari says the Purosangue is not an SUV but an FUV—a Ferrari Utility Vehicle.

Underneath that long hood lives a 6.5 L naturally aspirated V12, but mounted back in the chassis such that this is technically a front-mid engined layout. That contributes to the 49:51 front-to-rear weight ratio, as does the use of a transaxle gearbox for the rear wheels (an eight-speed, dual-clutch box); a separate power transfer unit at the front of the engine drives the front wheels, for this is an all-wheel drive Ferrari. But make no mistake, it’s a substantial one, too, befitting that massive 715 hp (533 kW), 528 lb-ft (716 Nm) engine: 195.8 inches (4,973 mm) long, 79.8 inches (2,028 mm) wide, 62.6 inches (1,589 mm) tall, with a 118.1-inch (3,018 mm) wheelbase and a 4,784 lbs (2,170 kg) curb weight.

c76e20d9149fa760: For most of the last century, T. rex was pictured as a sluggish, tail-dragging reptile that had to warm up in the sun before it could go anywhere. Then, further research changed that view, replacing it with the active, bird-like animal shown in the movie Jurassic Park. But whether T. rex used warm blood to power that activity remained a question. Now we might have gotten closer to an answer.

A team of researchers led by Randon J. Flores and Robert A. Eagle, geochemists at the University of California, Los Angeles, has measured the T. rex body temperature by analyzing its teeth. This dental thermometer read about 36° Celsius—roughly the body temperature of a modern elephant.

Paleontologists have long argued about dinosaur physiology based on indirect evidence like bone microstructure, growth rates, and where fossils turn up on the map. Some studies suggested many dinosaurs were endotherms, generating their own body heat like birds and mammals. Others argued that each lineage may have had its own thermal strategy.
c8b1edd33ed5a316: Microsoft has a problem not entirely of its own making: The time it takes to bring a system back up to date after a few months of slumber. The company is keen to talk up how efficient it plans to make Windows. Not a day goes by without either a Microsoft representative or a fan insisting that Windows 11 is a lot snappier now than it used to be. (Usually they skirt the unfortunate truth that the Windows of yesteryear generally flies on modern hardware compared with the lumbering of today's software). Microsoft recently claimed that it is working to shrink Windows' footprint to the point where 8 GB would be enough to run things acceptably. We can only hope that one shard of light piercing the gloom of today's memory shortages and rising prices is that developers might prioritize efficient RAM use alongside slinging more ads or adding features few users require. However, this vulture's experience this week indicates that there is another area that needs addressing, and that is the number of updates slung out by vendors, and not just Microsoft. A few days ago, I wrote a story about a new way to skip the Microsoft account requirement during setup for the Home edition of Windows 11. At The Register, we like to test these claims thoroughly, so I fired up an x64 Windows laptop to check them out on real hardware, which is where the problems began. We've written before about the curse of updates, but this machine was running Windows 11 and had been up to date less than a year ago. How long could it take to get to the point where it would boot without Windows Update bleating about missed patches? The answer: about seven hours. Along with the huge array of updates for Windows components and the inevitable insistence that a new version of Microsoft's flagship operating system was needed, there were multiple firmware and driver updates and plenty of restarts. And, of course, there was the progress bar of lies and the percentage counter of deceit. In the decades since Microsoft first inflicted progress bars on Windows users, it has singularly failed to make them accurately reflect the, er, progress. "Yeah, so I'm going to stick at 65 percent for about an hour and then jump to 98 percent in 30 seconds before hanging there for another hour. Lol." That this behavior has endured for decades is beyond disappointing. Redmond is far from the only offender, but Windows' ubiquity makes it one of the most visible. To be clear, this was an ordinary Windows device, running a production version of the operating system. It just hadn't been turned on for a few months. The experience highlights a challenge Microsoft and its vendors must address. It's great that, at long last, people are considering code efficiency rather than simply flinging more hardware at badly written applications to make them run acceptably. But attention must also be paid to the constant flow of updates that seem to stem from an "ah well, we can always fix it in production" attitude that pervades the tech industry. Several years ago, the chief of a DevOps project was baffled when I asked him about testing and validation before release. Surely unit testing was sufficient? And the joy of modern development practices meant that if problems arose, an update could be swiftly rolled out. All of which assumes customers will tolerate continual updates, and a potential hours-long wait if, for some reason, they give it a few months between updates. The tech industry is waking up to the need for efficiencies, or at the very least Microsoft is. It also needs to deal with the scourge of update tsunamis. It's all well and good to brag about making your software run on limited resources until an interminable wait undermines the boast while the various widgets and components of a device insist on spending hours giving themselves a thorough update. Shaving a few seconds off the startup time means nothing if there are pages of updates awaiting the unwary. ®

d78905474687e96c: From Chin Yee Mun

According to demographic transition theory (DDT), birth rates are expected to decline as a society shifts from an agrarian to an industrial economy, with this change affecting the size and composition of its population.
In an agrarian society, birth rates are high but are also accompanied by high death rates. As a result, population growth was minimal in most societies at the time.
This began to change as societies moved towards industrial economies. Better healthcare meant lower death rates, while birth rates remained more or less unchanged.

However, this trend eventually began to change. Besides better healthcare, industrialisation brought urbanisation, improved education, modern lifestyles and, most importantly, changes in values. Individualism took root as industrialisation empowered such a culture.

As a result, birth rates began to decline. This is particularly visible among Malaysian Chinese. The decline in childbirth among the Chinese in Malaysia, as well as elsewhere, became apparent in the 1980s. The total fertility rate (TFR) among Malaysian Chinese women was 3.3 in 1980. Two decades later, it had fallen to 2.1.

According to the WHO, a TFR of 2.1 is generally considered the replacement level needed for a population to maintain its size over the long term, assuming no migration. If the TFR falls below this level, a population will eventually begin to shrink and age.
Unfortunately, the Chinese community’s TFR has continued to decline. Last year, the TFR among Chinese women was 0.8.

Reports from the statistics department show that the number of Malaysian Chinese has been declining since 2021. Migration is certainly one factor contributing to this decline, but the bigger factor is likely the fall in the Chinese birth rate.
In other words, the Chinese population is now at the “free-fall” stage. In DDT, this refers to a possible fifth stage.

According to the theory, some societies may see birth rates increase after the fourth stage, while others may continue to experience declines. Unfortunately, DDT describes these trends but does not explain why they occur.
Based on my analysis of the Chinese community in Malaysia, as well as Chinese communities across the Sinosphere, I believe I can offer an explanation.
For me, the Chinese have moved into hypermodernity. I took this term from Gilles Lipovetsky, who defined hypermodernity as an era characterised by the following:
Hyper-individualism: An intense focus on personal freedom, self-realisation and immediate gratification.
Hyper-consumerism: Consumption driven not only by status, but also by emotional experiences, health, wellness and constant novelty.
Hyper-technologisation: Technology operating at breakneck speed, redefining time, space and human interaction.

At present, particularly among younger Chinese people, hyper-individualism is increasingly evident. This can be observed in their lifestyles, including the pursuit of immediate gratification and an aversion to responsibilities. They are also driven by hyper-consumerism, sometimes consuming beyond their means.
Technology appears to reinforce these tendencies by connecting people while constantly exposing them to new products and experiences designed to provide gratification.
When such behaviour takes hold, values change.
Chinese values traditionally prioritised family, with starting a family often seen as a natural responsibility.

In a hypermodern world, however, this view is becoming less influential. Family can instead be perceived as a burden or an obstacle to personal gratification and the consumption of goods and experiences that provide satisfaction.

Hence, a subculture of anti-familism appears to be growing among Chinese youth. It may have been started by individuals who view the family as an institution that undermines happiness and life satisfaction.
This can be seen on social media, where various videos encourage singlehood and portray marriage as awful or destructive.
When such messages become widespread, they can validate the idea that it is acceptable to remain single, not start a family and not have children.

Hyper-consumerism may also contribute to the perception that raising children is financially unaffordable. For many Chinese families, raising a child is associated with spending on expensive preschools, private schools and universities.
While wanting to provide the best for one’s children is commendable, these expectations can also become a convenient justification for choosing not to have children.

This problem is now spreading to other communities in Malaysia. The Indian community faces a similar problem, with declining birth rates and a shrinking population. Similar trends are also emerging among Malays and the Bumiputera communities in Sabah and Sarawak.

In my view, measures to address or at least contain this problem must go beyond financial incentives. Many developing countries do not face the same low-birth-rate problem, while the issue is particularly pronounced in upper-middle-income and developed countries.
Hence, the problem is not simply about income. It is about the broader social ecology.

We need to bring hypermodernity under control by addressing hyper-individualism, hyper-consumerism and the influence of technology, particularly social media. At the same time, other measures could help create an environment that is more conducive to starting families and having children.
For example, childcare costs could be reduced by allowing childcare centres to operate in or near workplaces.

Tax and financial incentives could also be introduced as part of a broader effort to improve this social ecology, making it more conducive to forming families and having children rather than relying on them as the primary means of addressing the problem.
Chin Yee Mun is an associate professor and the director of the Tun Tan Cheng Lock Institute of Social Studies at Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman.

31fed871e382cf10: Reactions to former prime minister Najib Razak’s conditional pardon have come in fast and furious, with some singling out Pakatan Harapan and DAP’s Hannah Yeoh for abandoning their stance on graft.

Yeoh, as the federal territories minister, sits on the Federal Territories Pardons Board that met on Friday morning. The Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, who presides over the meeting, granted Najib the conditional pardon, according to the legal affairs division of the Prime Ministers' Department.
But before we, the general public, turn into keyboard warriors waiting to pounce on what we deem to be a gross injustice, there are a few things to bear in mind.

First, Najib did not obtain a full pardon. Umno was pushing for it, but Sultan Ibrahim, in his wisdom, thought otherwise. Najib still has to serve his reduced sentence, at home, once he pays RM50 million up front.
This decision is extremely fair when considering that Najib could have received a full pardon like the one obtained by Anwar Ibrahim in 2018.
Second, the conditional pardon is for the conviction in the SRC International case, not for the 1MDB case. This means Najib isn’t going galavanting any time soon.
Third — and this cannot be emphasised enough -- the power to grant pardons lies with the King and not any sitting government.

Yes, government representatives sit on the pardons board, and that is all we know. We will never know what is discussed, as the minutes of the meeting are classified under the Official Secrets Act. And because we don’t know the discussions that took place, it would be unwise to make assumptions.
It is for this very reason we should not be pointing fingers at the government or Yeoh. The King makes his decision based on the discussions held. End of story.
With these three things out of the way, Najib’s conditional pardon however raises two concerns.
One: does house arrest mean he would be able to receive visitors? Would he have access to social media? Access which would allow him to plan his political comeback?
It doesn't sit right with me if Najib is allowed to receive visitors or access to social media. Irrespective of who you are, the rules and regulations of a house arrest should apply equally.
Two: there will no doubt be politicians who want to resign from government because of Najib’s conditional pardon.
Principled maybe, but not necessarily right. Such a sharp response could be construed as defiance of the King’s will. A move that would undoubtedly whip up a racial and religious rhetoric.
So stay on. And if you need to voice your grievances do so politely. The same goes for those who want to hold demonstrations. Don’ go overboard as it would only sully the royal institution.

Politicians being placed under house arrest isn’t a new phenomenon in the world. Prominent figures in other countries have undergone a similar sentence. Najib only has the “honour” of being the first in Malaysia.
Mind you, he wasn’t pardoned for his crimes, and as a citizen I can live with that.
